News.title: Inside Essex Boys’ final weeks… £1k-a-day coke binges, teen death & triple drug deal betrayal to ‘become millionaires’
News.content:
IF the mythology surrounding the Essex Boys is to be believed, they were sophisticated gangsters, comparable to The Krays, heading an 80-strong firm and had connections to the celebrity world.

The truth couldn’t be any further away, according to former colleague Bernard O’Mahoney, now 66, who reveals the reality of the three drug dealers viciously assassinated back in 1995 and the fateful missteps of their final weeks.



“Herein lies the problem,” he tells us. “Until they were shot, nobody had heard of them, not even in Basildon, yet, they were being compared to The Krays and mafia dons.

“The Krays were running nightclubs, slot machines and race track schemes, hitting people for money, while the Essex Boys were idiots in a nightclub doing absolutely zilch.”

Their fictionalised legacy has been moulded through countless documentaries and at least 14 feature films, including one starring Sean Bean, and a new movie out later this month.



Rise Of The Footsoldier: Retribution, out on August 28, is the seventh in the franchise, which has starred big names like Vinnie Jones, Tamer Hassan and Craig Fairbrass, and gives the Essex Boys’ story a dramatised make-over.

However, the final weeks of ill-fated Pat Tate, Tony Tucker and Craig Rolfe was rather cinematic – before they were lured to Workhouse Lane, in Rettendon, for a “brutal gangland execution”, blasted to death by an assassin hidden in the bushes.

Bernard knew the Boys from working security at Basildon’s notorious nightclub Raquel’s, where the crooks peddled ecstasy, and watched first-hand as their destructive behaviour ensured they would “never make it to the old folks’ home”.

He alleges a botched £120,000 weed deal from overseas, hitman threats, the death of a teen and betraying dangerous gangsters and a seasoned crook all contributed to their death, revealing all to The Sun.

Bernard says: “Tate was the worst of the lot, he was a bully, who picked on the wrong people. Within six months of knowing Tucker, he managed to get himself shot twice, the latter fatally.



“I’ve been a nuisance for 66 years and no one has ever shot me. It shows what bullies they were. They weren’t The Krays, they weren’t gangsters, they were absolute idiots.”

Bernard first met Tucker at Raquel’s in 1993 and watched him change dramatically after meeting his fellow Essex Boys – especially in their final weeks due to stressful events and drug use.

He recalls Tucker, 38, being a “squeaky clean” carpenter-by-trade without any convictions or arrests, who drove a Ford Grenada, before becoming a £40-a-night doorman and later setting up his own security firm.

In August 1994, Tucker met Rolfe, 26, and Tate, 37, through a mutual friend at a Southend cafe and the latter two “tried to impress each other, through bullying tactics”. Soon they were working together.

Rolfe was a violent cocaine addict, who was born in Holloway Prison, meanwhile Tate – then newly out of prison – was an 18-stone man mountain, who abused heroin, cocaine, cannabis and steroids.



The trio began dealing ecstasy at Raquel’s due to Tucker’s inroads there with Bernard, who ran security there.

Tate and Rolfe were the enforcers inside, simultaneously flooding the dancefloor with drugs, while also beating-up anyone trying to sell on their patch.

Bernard says: “They really were robbers and drug dealers. They coaxed people into the nightclub, slapped them across the face for dealing, punched them up and threw them out.



“They kept the drugs too. They were bullies. That’s not a way to go about business in that world, you’ll hit the wrong guy and whoever he works for will be a lot more powerful.”

Their plans were derailed when, in November 2024, Tate threatened the family of crooked associate, Steve ‘Nipper’ Ellis, who shot him in the arm, leading to prison stints for them both.

Paula Jackson, Tate’s girlfriend, told The Terry Stone Connection: “His arm was like blown open, you could see all the tendons in there. It was awful.”

She claims he shot him through his toilet window, while he was sitting on the loo, with a “two-bob Smith and Weston, 200-year-old antique gun”.



While in hospital, police found Tate was concealing a handgun, a violation of his parole terms, meaning he was jailed until November 1995 – just weeks before his murder.

Upon his release, Tate and Tucker were spending nearly £1,000 a day on crack cocaine according to Bernard, who said: “They were out of their heads all the time.

“They were like zombies. Smoking that shit, then going to sleep, waking up and doing it again. They transformed into psychotic bullies, who couldn’t be reasoned with.

“They were doing absolutely zilch, a couple of idiots sat in the nightclub doing drugs all of the time. They never stepped in if there was a fight at Raquel’s.”



Tate’s drug-induced volatility was best highlighted by him beating up a pizza shop manager for using the wrong toppings and even threatening his mother.

Roughly three weeks before the killings, tragedy struck when teenage Leah Betts, who was celebrating her 18th birthday at Raquel’s, died as a result of taking one of the gang’s ecstasy pills and drinking too much water.

The death was a massive story and front page news on most national newspapers.

Bernard recalls “the world’s media descended” with TV crews from the BBC, Sky News, ITV and Sweden surrounding Raquel’s. He says: “It was a drug dealer’s worst nightmare.



“Tate was furious and yelled, ‘Get this f***ing sorted! This was the same weekend they did a dud cannabis deal. He was going off his head because everything was going wrong.

“I told him, ‘When the police come they’ll help us’ and he went f***ing mental, threatening, ‘You can’t f***ing talk to them.’ I told him I would and I did.”

Bernard unsuccessfully tried to source one of the tablets for police, much to the anger of Tate and Tucker, who began boasting to others that they would kill him.

“They started ringing people up, saying ‘I’m going to f***ing shoot him’,” he says. “I’d heard it all before by then and knew they didn’t have it in them.”



Despite dismissing the threat, it seems they had planned a hit as Bernard was summoned to a police station. Cops told him: “We have intelligence that you’re going to be shot. You need to take this seriously.”

Five hours later, unbeknown to Bernard – as he had hopped on a train with his family to get away – the Essex Boys were dead.

According to the bouncer, it all stemmed from missteps linked to Tucker and Tate’s plan to import drugs themselves.

When he was told about the plot, it was a shock to Bernard, who remarked to them: “F***ing hell, are you for real?”



He added: “I wouldn’t have trusted going through a drive-thru with them, let alone them importing drugs.”

The Essex Boys raised £120,000 through a consortium of dangerous local criminals to pay the gang’s future killers Michael Steele and Jack Wholmes – who Tate first met in prison – to smuggle the drugs for them.

“But when the cannabis arrived from Amsterdam, much of it was dud cannabis,” Bernard says. “They were like, ‘This gear is sh*t’ and threatened Steele telling him to get their money back.

“What Steele didn’t know was that around a third of the cannabis, £46,000-worth, was good gear. Tate and the Essex Boys sold this in secret.”



Bernard says Steele only found out upon getting the money back from the weed sellers. He had been duped. Yet Steele returned the full £120,000, which Tate held for another deal.

Bernard added: “Tate was fuming because the deal had gone wrong and they supplied s*** gear. So as well as keeping the £46,000 good bit, he told the investors that Steele didn’t get a refund for the money.

“So a lot of bad s*** going on between these two groups. Tate told one of the investors, ‘I’ll get Steel on his knees, if he doesn’t give me the money, I’ll shoot his f***ing head.”

The threat to kill him, ripping him off of the proceeds from the £48,000 of weed and withholding his part of the £120,000 were the three sleights that led to the Essex Boys’ killing, Bernard says.



Whomes and Steele conjured up a plan. They told the gang they would fly £1million-worth of cocaine onto a farmer’s field in the sleepy village of Rettendon for them to sell-on.

To ensure all issues were avoided they would do a dummy run – in reality, that night on Workhouse Lane, they would be assassinated.

True to form, Tate had no intention of playing fair. Bernard says: “They planned to bash up the guy who flew in the coke, take the coke and split it three ways.

“They were greedy, jumping for joy, thinking they would be millionaires. They even booked an 8pm meal to celebrate.”



That night, Steele met the trio at a Hungry Horse pub in Raleigh, got into their car and he directed them to the field. Upon reaching the farmer’s gate near the field, Steele got out to open it.

Bernard continues: “Whomes comes out of the hedges, leans into the car with the shotgun and bang, bang, bang. Goodnight dear.

“That was The Essex Boys finished, and Steele and Whomes finished too. ”

Whomes spent 23 years behind bars until he was released in 2021. Steele was let out just last year after serving 27 years. Both always maintained their innocence.

Bernard struggles to understand the enduring mythology surrounding the Essex Boys today, insisting the dramatised creations of them were “pure fiction, they didn’t exist”.



He adds: “In the films, they had beautiful girls and flashy cars. I assure you that wasn’t the case, they lived in council houses and drove average cars. Their myth is blown way out of proportion.”

As for the legacy of the Essex Boys, while visiting Retendon, a homeowner, who would only speak through her RingDoor claimed she “knew them personally”.

After apologising for her loss, tellingly, she stated: “No, no, no, don’t be sorry. The world is a much better place since they have gone.”

News.title: Body found in search for missing man, 28, who vanished two weeks ago
News.content:
TRAGIC END Body found in search for missing man, 28, who vanished two weeks ago

THE body of a missing 28-year-old man who vanished two weeks ago has been found by cops.

Kacper Cichor, from Braunstone, Leicester, was last seen on July 21 and was reported missing the following day.



A desperate search was sparked for Kacper in the following days.

Cops have now sadly confirmed that his body has been found, said Leicestershire Police.



Kacper’s next of kin have been informed and are being supported by officers.

The force have said the tragic incident is not being treated as suspicious.

A spokesperson for the police said: “Police have confirmed that a body has been found as a result of a missing person investigation to find Kacper Cichor.

“Kacper, aged 28 and from Braunstone, was last seen on Tuesday 21 July and was reported missing the following day.

“The incident is not being treated as suspicious but officers believe that the person found is Kacper.

“His next of kin have been informed and we ask for privacy for his family and friends at this difficult time.



“Thank you to all the public who assisted in this investigation.”

Kacper attended Mansfield House police station in Leicester city centre on July 21 where he handed in some property, according to police.

He was then reported to have been seen in Webster Road, near Braunstone Park, at around 2.30pm that day.

As part of the investigation police released CCTV images showing him wearing a burgundy T-shirt, black jeans and grey sliders.

News.title: In-N-Out shooter, 24, is named after killing three and injuring seven in horrific drive-thru massacre
News.content:
A GUNMAN who killed three people at an In-N-Out burger drive-thru in Idaho has been named.

Chad Williams, 24, went on the horror rampage at the burger chain in Twin Falls before turning the gun on himself.



Terrifying footage showed Williams storm a shopping complex armed with a camouflaged AR-15-style rifle and let off a barrage of shots.

He killed three people, including a beloved employee, and injured seven others.



Two were left in critical condition, three others were described as stable, and two more have been discharged.

Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said Williams acted alone.



He praised a brave bystander armed with a handgun and off-duty officer who both fired at Williams during the incident.

Hicks said: “We believe their actions helped drive the suspect away from the scene, preventing further casualties.”

In a statement on Sunday, In-N-Out President Lynsi Snyder paid tribute to a “beautiful” employee who died in the tragedy.

She wrote: “My heart is broken, my chest is heavy, my eyes burn from the tears I’ve shed.



“We lost one of our beautiful Associates tonight. She was taking care of our most important asset – our customers, and her life was taken by a disgusting human who doesn’t value the lives of others or his own.

“He shot both on our property and off, and ended his life shortly after he took the precious lives of our Associate and Customers, innocent people who never saw it coming.”

The only victim to be identified so far is Terry Dudley.



The company that he works for, North Star Taxi, said he has “a very long road ahead of him.”

Terry was charging his Tesla when he was shot in the back twice, according to a GoFundMe page.

A statement on the fundraiser read: “Our community experienced the kind of tragedy that changes lives forever.

“A senseless act of violence took the lives of innocent people, left many others critically injured, and shattered countless families in an instant.

“Our hearts are with every victim and every loved one who is now facing unimaginable grief and uncertainty.



“In a matter of moments, an ordinary day became a nightmare that no family should ever have to endure.”

The page, which was set up to help “tenacious, compassionate, kind hearted” Terry, has raised more than $8,000 so far.

Police found Williams’ body in an area near the restaurant.

Bullets began ringing out at around 3pm local time, with shocking footage showing dozens of people fleeing for their lives.

Williams drove up to the chain’s drive-thru before exiting a white vehicle and retrieving a rifle from the trunk.



Wearing a black T-shirt and blue trousers, he was seen walking through the car park before shooting through a Tesla‘s windscreen.

Someone in an In-N-Out uniform was later filmed dragging a person, also uniformed, bleeding from a gunshot wound in her chest across the parking lot.

Twin Falls resident Haley Dodaro, 43, was having lunch in In-N-Out with her mum when she saw people running across the street.

“People were running out crying and screaming”, she said.

Officials were still working on notifying the family members of victims.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Apart from Terry, names, ages and other details of those wounded in the shooting have not been released.

The FBI confirmed it would be assisting in the ongoing investigation.

News.title: Why John Healey must avoid becoming the second Healey to send Britain’s finances off the rails
News.content:
HISTORY has a habit of coming back to haunt our politicians.

Fifty years after Denis ­Healey’s policies plunged ­Britain into economic turmoil, the nation’s finances now lie in the hands of another Chancellor called Healey.



Like his bushy-browed predecessor, John Healey faces strikingly similar challenges — stagnant growth, high inflation and rocketing oil prices.

But his mission could not be simpler: Don’t repeat the catastrophic mistakes that pushed Britain to the brink of bankruptcy half a century ago.



In 86 days’ time, he will give us the clearest indication of whether he has learned the lessons of history when he delivers the first Budget for Andy Burnham’s new government.

The Yorkshireman must utilise his blunt honesty and frugality to confront the harsh economic realities facing us.



His first tasks will be to force big-spending ministers to tighten their belts, tame the out-of-control welfare bill and rebuild our worn-out defences.

With an extra £13billion a year required to meet our Nato commitments, he will have to convince Labour MPs of the need to divert cash from benefits to bombs.

There is only one piece of advice from his former office-holder that John Healey should heed.

It’s a well-known phrase coined by Denis which goes: “The first rule of holes — when you are in one, stop digging.”



Unfortunately, Denis Healey didn’t follow his own advice. He was a “Silly Billy”, as TV mimic Mike Yarwood would say.

Inflation was at 15 per cent when Denis was appointed Chancellor in 1974.

Within a year, it hit 27 per cent — one of the highest rates in the developed world.

The excessive wage demands of militant trade unions, coupled with relentless pandering to Labour’s hard Left only made matters worse.

But it was his tax and spend instincts which turned crisis into catastrophe.



Vowing to squeeze the rich “until the pips squeak”, Denis Healey increased income tax to a historic peak of 83 per cent, with tax on investment income hitting 98 per cent.

It scared off investors and led to the brain drain of senior doctors and scientists, while cultural icons such as the Rolling Stones and Sir Rod Stewart became tax exiles.

Despite soaking the rich, he was still spending billions more than he received in taxes, and 50 years ago next month the chickens came home to roost.



On September 28, 1976, Denis Healey was sipping a G&T in the VIP lounge at Heathrow on his way to the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund, in Manila, when he received an urgent message from the Treasury.

Officials told him financial investors were selling the Pound because they feared its value would drop even further.

He abandoned the flight and rushed back to the office. Days later, he went cap in hand to the IMF for a £2.2billion bailout — about £20.5billion in today’s money.

It was the largest request it had received at that time.

The severe restrictions attached to the loan infuriated the unions and the Labour Left and set the stage for the Winter of Discontent of 1978-79, when widespread strike action led to fuel and food shortages, the dead left unburied and rubbish piled high in the streets.



It took two years of free market economics under Margaret Thatcher to restore Britain’s economic balance.

That’s why, after two weeks in the job, John Healey should take a break from Treasury spreadsheets and glance at the history books. He shares the same name, the same party and a similar massive headache to Denis.

But he can’t afford to make the same mistakes as his namesake fellow Yorkshire MP.

His first duty will be to lay down the law to Cabinet colleagues, backed by Burnham, that there is no new money for any spending pledges. This means reining in the people-pleasing Prime Minister and his unfunded giveaways, too.

Our new PM’s 86p-a-week cut on household energy bills, £2 cap on bus fares and help for pub and music venues has already landed the Chancellor with a combined bill of £1.5billion.



Some estimates put the cost of Mr Burnham’s policy proposals at £96billion — equivalent to £4,300 in extra tax for every family.

Mr Healey has to break the Labour cycle of promise, borrow and spend.

He must show a clear path to stop £3trillion of government debt rising and for it eventually to fall, control inflation and turbocharge economic growth.



That means getting a grip on the bloated welfare budget and banning large, unfunded spending increases.

The simple truth is one that politicians hate to hear.

You can’t keep spending money you haven’t earned.

You can’t tax businesses into creating jobs.

And you can’t borrow your way to prosperity.



The wealth has to come first.

If John Healey bears that in mind, he might avoid becoming the second Healey remembered for sending Britain’s finances off the rails.

ANDY BURNHAM showed solidarity with President Zelensky by wearing a black T-shirt and jacket for his meeting with the Ukrainian leader.

I wonder whether he’ll have the nerve to dress down when he finally gets an audience with Donald Trump.



TONY BLAIR famously announced that his three priorities for government were “education, education and education”.

But it seems the job of running our schools is less of a prize and more like the ministerial equivalent of detention.

After removing Bridget Phillipson from the post of Education Secretary, Andy Burnham offered the job to Ed Miliband’s brother, David, along with a seat in the Lords.

He politely declined.

Burnham then turned to Rachel Reeves, ­suggesting she might take it as a ­consolation prize after being axed as ­Chancellor. She passed, too.



Only at the third attempt did Labour’s ­deputy leader Lucy Powell agree to take on the brief.

But even then she wasn’t ­punching the air, as she had been hoping to land something bigger – Deputy PM, ­perhaps.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

That’s four noses put out of joint over what was once a plum Cabinet job.

Or, as Pink Floyd almost put it: We don’t need no Education Secretary.

News.title: Labour blasted after 160k businesses close in six months under weight of National Insurance hikes & extra red tape
News.content:
LABOUR has been blasted after 160,415 businesses closed in six months under the full weight of National Insurance hikes and extra red tape.

And business creation is at one of the lowest levels in a decade.



Ex-Chancellor Rachel Reeves’s £25billion tax grab made it more expensive to hire staff, while boosts to workers’ rights and the minimum wage were also said to have been factors.

Business openings in the first six months of the year stood at 157,980 — lower than during Covid, and at anytime since the first half of 2023.



Straight after the pandemic, the figure peaked at 193,245.

Shadow Chancellor Mel Stride told The Sun: “Labour don’t understand business.

“Their new regulations and higher taxes are destroying jobs and punishing the businesses that drive our economy.”

Shadow Business Secretary Andrew Griffith said some entrepreneurs had fled the country and others were now thinking twice before making a move.

He added: “The drought of new businesses opening in Britain is every bit as barren as the dry weather.”

The Lib Dems analysed official figures to reveal the business crisis.



The party wants a new deal with Europe, claiming it would cut regulations.

Economic spokesperson Daisy Cooper said: “Too many budding entrepreneurs will look at the Government’s crushing jobs tax and anti-growth agenda and be put off even trying to get their business off the ground.”

Britain’s economy shrank in April amid the Iran War, continuing to have an impact on energy prices in particulary. It grew by 0.1 per cent in May, according to the ONS.

News.title: Taxpayers have forked out enough for promises on migrant boats — they want to see results
News.content:
Show us results

IN the past decade, Britain has handed over £1billion to France as an incentive to stop the migrant boats.

But what have taxpayers got for their money?



Since 2018, more than 200,000 have crossed the Channel in flimsy dinghies — enough to populate Portsmouth — while French police simply shrugged their shoulders and looked on.

You’d be forgiven for thinking they had been told not to try too hard because they’re glad to see the back of them.



The more money they get the less they do to intercept boats in shallow water.

Barely a third of attempted crossings have been thwarted by French police since a lucrative three-year funding deal was signed in April.

The number of migrants arriving by small boats has topped 2,000 in the two weeks since Andy Burnham became PM.

Last Wednesday, 752 landed, the highest number in a single day this year.

We now learn it costs £8,000 for every migrant they stop — most of whom probably hop on the next boat out anyway.

The money would be better spent on a proper deterrent like reviving the Rwanda deportation scheme — sending Labour’s open borders backbenchers into meltdown in the process.



Uncontrolled migration is having a devastating impact on wages and will make British workers £2,500 a year worse off by 2031, according to Tory analysis.

Sooner or later Mr Burnham is going to have to confront the thorny issue head-on.

He won’t solve the problem by talking about buses or his favourite pub snacks on social media or telling us that “much more needs to be done”.

It’s two weeks since he entered No10 on a pledge to restore hope in politics.

Taxpayers have forked out enough for promises. They want to see results.



Tin eared

THE shocking scenes in Ceuta should be a wake-up call for world leaders.

Some 60,000 migrants entered the tiny Spanish territory from Morocco, in Europe’s biggest ever border breach.

It left 72 people dead and caused alarm among national leaders. But not so Spain’s PM.

As a sea search for bodies continued, Pedro Sanchez left for a two-week holiday with his wife in Lanzarote.

In a callous disregard for the victims, he took to social media to share his soundtrack of music by Madonna, Charli XCX and the Rolling Stones.



Europe’s border crisis demands serious leadership — not a playlist.

Get to business

BRITISH business is stuck in a vicious circle of high taxes and sluggish growth.

New ventures are starting up at the lowest rate in a decade.

More than 160,000 firms closed last year after crippling Labour National Insurance hikes.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In 12 weeks’ time, new Chancellor John Healey can turn his first Budget into a lifeline for business.



By undoing the damage inflicted by his predecessor.

News.title: Railway station just a stone’s throw from Del Boy’s famous flat to produce Britain’s first-ever station wine
News.content:
BRITAIN’S wine industry has shown it is on track – after the nation’s strangest vineyard sprung up at an urban railway station close to Del Boy’s south London manor.

Chateau Denmark Hill – at the station in Camberwell – will be sticking the cork in their white wine from their 22 Bacchus vines, grown metres from the busy tracks.



It will make it the first wine to be produced at a railway station in the UK – and a sign of Britain’s changing climate as most the nation basks in yet another heatwave.

And the tiny vineyard is less than two miles from Del Boy and Rodney’s fictional Only Fools and Horses flat in Peckham where he would often exclaim: “Chateauneuf du Pape.”



Commuters are expected to be able to enjoy vin du pays when the wine is ready to be uncorked as early as next year.

Local Keith Griffiths, 41, a copywriter said: “I walked past without noticing it, then spotted it from the signs – and now cannot wait to try it.

“It’s amazing to have a little vineyard in Camberwell and is a great use of space.

“I supposed it is also one benefit of warming temperatures.

“It is the sort of entrepreneurial spirit that would make Del Boy proud.”

Winemakers at the station – next to busy King’s Hospital and in one of the capital’s most hectic areas – wrote on their Instagram: “This year will be our first wine producing year at the station.”



In another post, they added: “The dream of sipping a glass of wine, grown right here in Camberwell, is becoming a reality… making history as they work on the first ever vineyard in a UK station.”

Camberwell is a densely populated area just two miles south of central London with former inhabitants including ex-England football ace Jadon Sancho, comedian Jenny Éclair and ex PM Boris Johnson and his wife Carrie.

Rail firm GTR – the nation’s largest railway franchise which owns Southern, Thameslink, Great Northern and Gatwick Express – has helped fund the vineyard.

The project is being run by the Camberwell society, who have named it ‘Chateau Denmark Hill Station’.

Winemakers reclaimed a tiny bank just two metres from the busy station platform and planted 22 Bacchus vines.



They have all now budded wine and are ready to be harvested.

A new sign proudly announces itself as “the first ever vineyard at a UK station”.

Wine-making is one of the UK’s fastest-growing new industries with over 1,100 active sites nationwide due to warmer summer weather.

Around 16.5million bottles of wine are produced across the country every year with most being made in Kent, Sussex and Hampshire – with many bottles of sparkling wine rivalling the best from France’s acclaimed champagne region.

News.title: Afghan murder suspect ‘was cleaner in building where Brit found dead in suitcase was staying’ in Athens
News.content:
AN AFGHAN suspect arrested over the death of a Brit woman was reportedly a cleaner in the building where she was staying.

Elisabeth Ross, 38, was found stuffed inside a suitcase at an abandoned building in central Athens two weeks ago.



After a major manhunt, Greek cops said they had detained a 26-year-old Afghan man “for intentional homicide, robbery and violation of the law [regarding] weapons”.

The suspect claimed the Scotswoman was already dead when he found her, but police have been working on the theory that Elisabeth was killed in the flat.



George Kalliakmanis, the president of the Attica Police Officers’ Union, told The Times: “[The suspect] and his wife worked as the cleaners of the building where Elisabeth lived.

“He allegedly killed her, took her bank card, and put her body in a suitcase or a box. He then transported it to the abandoned building using a trolley.

“Once there, he realised the suitcase he had used would likely contain his fingerprints, so he transferred the body into a second suitcase, trying to be more careful to avoid leaving prints.”

The possibility Elisabeth was suffocated is being “seriously contemplated” given the lack of evident injuries on her body, a well placed source told the Sun.



Police found a replica pistol and a knife in a raid of the suspect‘s home, which is a ten-minute walk from the derelict block where Elisabeth’s body was found.

He was reportedly identified on CCTV using her credit cards to withdraw money from ATMs.

Cops were able to find fingerprints and track the suspect down to Arachova, a mountain village in central Greece.



Elisabeth’s phone was used to send messages and mislead her loved ones until her identity was made public on July 29.

Her dad, a lawyer from Edinburgh, said he received texts for up to two weeks after her death.

Messages sent to family and friends claimed that she needed to take some time for herself and wanted to be alone for a while.

A Facebook post announcing that she was going to travel to Turkey was made on July 24, six days after her body was found, according to the Mail.

Elisabeth arrived in the Greek capital on a flight from Edinburgh on June 26.



A Greek couple who Elisabeth was staying with in Keratsini told cops she was going to stay with some Americans she knew in Kypseli.

But cops later revealed that they believed she used it as a cover story to visit the homeless community in central Athens without worrying her friends.

Elisabeth, known as Lisa, was reportedly seen chatting to homeless people close to an abandoned car park where they take drugs, drink and sleep rough.

She was a regular traveller to Greece and volunteered for One Heart – a charity which provides medical help for refugees from Afghanistan and Iran.

Her aunt, Anne Bangham, described her as a “beautiful loving and kind young lady”.



Greek authorities said her cause of death could be revealed in “days” as they fast-track crucial tests.

Tests on blood, urine and vital organ tissues will be key to determine if foul play was involved.

The Foreign and Commonwealth Office said earlier: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time.

“We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece.



“Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.”

News.title: 'Secret sleep condition caused me to gain 40lbs in six months despite healthy life'
News.content:
'Secret sleep condition caused me to gain 40lbs in six months despite healthy life'

Lex Banach couldn't figure out what was going on until she got her diagnosis

View 3 Images Lex Banach after she lost weight (Image: Lex Banach/SWNS)

A woman gained 40lbs in six months, despite eating and exercising the same as before.

‌



Lex Banach, 29, felt like she was going “insane” when she began to rapidly put on weight, despite eating well and going to the gym regularly. After suffering from brain fog and extreme fatigue, she went to the doctor and was told she had had sleep apnoea for three years, without her knowledge. The content creator, from Milwaukee, Wisconsin, began using a CPAP machine and lost 60lbs in a year.

‌



She said: “I felt insane for years because I didn’t know what was going on with my body. I was so confused; I was following the same nutrition plan and doing the same workouts.

‌



“I’ve always snored and always been a mouth breather. My doctor told me the weight gain was likely sleep apnoea.

“The test showed I stopped breathing every eight minutes. I was so relieved to finally have an answer, but surprised to hear it was only mild, considering how much it impacted me.”

View 3 Images Lex Banach put on 40lb despite having a good diet and doing exercise (Image: Lex Banach/SWNS)

‌



Lex is into fitness and in 2020 she lost 20lbs, taking her from 180lbs to her goal weight of 160lbs. She maintained this for a year, then in early 2021 she began to gain weight rapidly and put on 40lbs in the space of six months.

Confused, she decided to come off the birth control pill in 2022, as since she was eating the same and doing the same amount of exercise as before, she couldn’t think of any other reason for her weight gain.

“It was kind of a wellness trend at the time to come off the pill, but it didn’t change anything," she said. She then began to experience brain fog and extreme fatigue.

‌



“I had to nap every single day; I was just so exhausted all of the time," she said. She also began to struggle with impulse control.

“I would say I was just going to have one cookie, and then eat the whole container," she said. “I just didn’t feel like myself; I wasn’t bubbly anymore, and I kept snapping at my partner.”

Feeling down, Lex went to the doctor for a therapy referral and was told she likely had anxiety and depression, as well as sleep apnoea. Sleep apnoea is when your breathing stops and starts while you sleep.

‌



Symptoms include mood swings, difficulty sleeping and fatigue and if not treated it can lead to serious problems, such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Lex’s doctor ordered her a sleep study, which records your heart rate, oxygen levels and breathing whilst you sleep.

She attached a sensor to her finger before bed and the device monitored her vitals while she slept. The test showed that Lex woke up 68 times during the night and she was diagnosed with mild sleep apnoea.

View 3 Images Lex Banach before and after she lost weight (Image: Lex Banach/SWNS)

Article continues below

Sleep apnoea can contribute to weight gain because disrupted sleep affects your metabolism, causes hormonal imbalance and affects your energy levels, leaving you less able to do physical activity. Following her diagnosis, Lex was given a CPAP machine in June 2023, which pumps air into a mask you wear over your nose and mouth while you sleep, to improve your breathing.

Within a few months, Lex started to see a change in her body and within a year she had lost 60lbs, bringing her weight down to 140lbs. In February 2024, she did a repeat study and was told by doctors that her sleep apnoea had reversed.

However, she had to return the CPAP machine in April 2024 and in May 2025, she began having symptoms of sleep apnoea again. As Lex no longer has health insurance, she hasn’t been able to access a CPAP machine again now that her symptoms have come back and has gained 20lbs. However, she is trying her best to manage her symptoms with meditation and yoga.

News.title: Dad accused of murdering six-month-old boy tells police he 'found it funny'
News.content:
Dad accused of murdering six-month-old boy tells police he 'found it funny'

Officals say it wasn't the first time the dad had used gardening tools to terrorise his own infant son - who has not been named and died in hospital in August 2024

View 3 Images (Image: Marion County Sheriff's Office)

A father has admitted to police that he 'found it funny' to allegedly torment his own son with a leaf blower, it has now been revealed.

James Westervelt, a 38-year-old Florida man, used a leaf blower to terrorise his own infant son on multiple occasions prior to the child's death at six months of age.

Westervelt admitted to police he 'found it funny' to use the high-powered gardening implement on his son. And it isn't the first time he had turned on the tot armed with a leaf blower: he also faces child abuse for tormenting his son at two months of age with the same power tool. That incident had left the child in significant distress and struggling to breathe.

The boy, who has not been named, died in hospital in August 2024 after he was admitted to hospital on life support. Doctors say the baby suffered blunt force trauma as a result of being over-bounced; injuries which the boy may have sustained at the hands of his own dad armed with the leaf blower.

View 3 Images The baby was allegedly terrorised with a leaf blower [file image] (Image: Alamy Stock Photo)

But, as well as admitting to investigators that the 38-year-old found the leaf blower attacks "funny", police now also say they have obtained footage of the Florida man recklessly blowing air at the boy in another incident prior to the one that wound up killing him.

As a result, Westerfelt has now also been hit with a first-degree murder charge for the death of the baby boy, in addition to already-pending child abuse charges.

The incident comes days after a toddler tragically lost his life after he was abandoned in a scalding hot bath by his mother’s boyfriend, who left the child to pick up drugs. During the shocking ordeal when the burns were found on the child - instead of administering medical attention, ointment was applied by the couple instead, leading to the boy's death. The horror occurred back in September 2023 while Sergio Mena, 34, was watching over Henry Wheatley-Brown – the one-year-old son of his girlfriend Samantha Garver, 36.

Article continues below

View 3 Images Henry Wheatley-Brown suffered terrible injuries before his death (Image: ABC7)

On the day of the tragic incident Mena was set to bathe the child and placed the toddler into the scalding bath. Mena then left the infant to pick up some methamphetamine and came back to find the boy screaming after being "severely burned." Mena then called the one-year-old’s mother who returned home later that evening. Prosecutors stated: "Despite Henry's extensive and life-threatening injuries, neither defendant sought medical care, instead attempting to treat the burns with over‑the‑counter ointment". The following day Mena and his girlfriend called emergency services stating Henry was suffering from "shallow breathing."

News.title: UK airport warning as 'departure lounge is worst place on Earth' to buy common item
News.content:
UK airport warning as 'departure lounge is worst place on Earth' to buy common item

An expert said it was a common error

View 3 Images It's easy to assume you're getting a good deal (Image: tupungato via Getty Images)

People who shop at duty free in airports are being told to think twice by an expert.

‌



Holidaymakers could end up paying 10 times more than they need to for perfume if they buy it at the airport instead of planning ahead, according to an expert. While many travellers still assume airport duty-free offers the best deals, UK fragrance research site ScentVerdict said the departure lounge was one of the worst places to buy perfume because shoppers are rushed into making expensive decisions.

‌



The biggest example is Tom Ford's Lost Cherry. A 100ml bottle typically retails for around £300, but analysis by ScentVerdict found 14 UK dupe brands selling their own interpretation for a median price of just £30 – around one tenth of the cost.

‌



Daniel Grimes, founder of ScentVerdict, said buying perfume at the airport was a mistake many travellers make.

He added: "The departure lounge is the worst place on Earth to buy perfume, because it is the one place where you are shopping against the clock. The 'duty-free' label does the persuading; you have not smelled the thing properly, and your flight is boarding.

"Decide before you fly, not at the gate. Take Tom Ford's Lost Cherry as an example.

‌



"It is around £300 at retail for 100ml; 14 different UK dupe houses sell their own version of it and the typical price is about £30 for the same 100ml, roughly a tenth.

"It will not be identical and you are not buying Tom Ford. But if what you want is that cherry-and-almond hit rather than the box it comes in, the maths is hard to argue with."

View 3 Images Daniel Grimes

‌



The findings suggest dupe fragrances tend to sell for broadly the same price regardless of how expensive the original designer bottle is. Across 10 of Britain's most popular fragrances, originals ranged from £89 to £310, while equivalent dupes typically sold for around £30.

The most extreme example remains Creed Aventus, one of the UK's best-known men's fragrances. A 100ml bottle retails for £310, while the median price of a comparable dupe is just £29.

Even fragrances with much lower retail prices show a similar pattern. Montblanc Explorer sells for around £89, while a typical dupe costs £25, suggesting dupe brands price according to what shoppers expect to pay rather than matching the original fragrance. Grimes said many people assume dupes simply undercut luxury brands by a percentage, but the figures suggest otherwise.

‌



He continued: "That flat £30 is the story. The dupe houses aren't pricing against the original at all. They charge what someone will pay for a dupe, and it barely shifts whether they're copying an £89 Montblanc or a £310 Creed.

"The saving isn't really a discount. It just tracks whatever the designer decided to charge."

He added that shoppers should still compare prices before deciding, as some designer fragrances are regularly discounted outside airports, narrowing the gap between the original and a dupe.

Article continues below

View 3 Images Fragance might not be best bought at the airport, according to an expert (Image: SolStock via Getty Images)

Retail prices for the designer fragrances were checked at John Lewis, Boots and The Perfume Shop on July 17, 2026, while dupe prices represent the median price charged across brands selling equivalent fragrances at each bottle size.

News.title: Pensions change 'accelerating' as new DWP update given
News.content:
Pensions change 'accelerating' as new DWP update given

An expert has explained what it means

View 3 Images The DWP has released new figures (Image: Mike Kemp, In Pictures via Getty Images)

Official figures published last week highlighted a seismic change in the UK’s retirement landscape.

‌



They showed that more pensioners were now having to cope without the guaranteed income that previous generations had enjoyed. When assessing private pensions accessed for the first time, the Department for Work & Pensions ( DWP ) found that the proportion of people receiving a lump sum or other Defined Contribution product rose from 37% (280,000) in the 2016/17 financial year to 49% (410,000) in the 2025/26 financial year.

‌



Samuel Mather-Holgate, managing director and Independent Financial Adviser at Mather and Murray Financial, explained what this means in plain English.

‌



He said: “Essentially, we are now transitioning from the gilt-edged ‘Defined Benefit’ pensions of old where income was guaranteed until death to pensions based on ‘Defined Contributions’, where a pot will last as long as it can and is at the mercy of markets. And it’s a shift that is accelerating.”

With a DB pension, the employer effectively guarantees the income a person will receive in retirement, whereas with a DC pension the income generated depends on the size of the pot and market performance, as well as fund fees. In short, the pensioner is vulnerable to how much they have saved and what markets do — rather than the employer.

View 3 Images Samuel Mather-Holgate

‌



Samuel added: “People with DB pensions, whether final salary or career-average, such as the NHS CARE scheme, have a security in retirement that most private sector workers will soon no longer enjoy. A generation of workers has effectively been switched from a retirement promise to a retirement savings account, often without fully understanding the difference.

“And this is the point at which a person’s failure to invest appropriately for their retirement comes home to roost as the State pension will prove woefully inadequate for most.”

Samuel said the UK was now entering the age of ‘pension inadequacy’, one where responsibility and risk had shifted from employers to individuals, many of whom simply haven’t saved enough to have the retirement they would have liked. While he accepted that auto-enrolment (AE) had been a major step forward, with millions now saving into pensions and receiving employer contributions, the minimum contributions many make through AE will simply not be enough to fund a retirement that could last for 30 or even 40 years.

‌



Samuel continued: “AE should be the starting point, not the whole retirement plan but, due to a lack of education around pensions, that is what it has become.”

Samuel urged people to put as much as they could into their workplace pension so that they could get the maximum benefit from the employer contributions. He said: “Failing to maximise matching contributions is effectively turning down part of your pay.”

He also urged people to review their pensions regularly, particularly after changing jobs, receiving a pay rise, divorcing, inheriting money or approaching retirement.

‌



View 3 Images The pensions landscape is changing (Image: Jacob Wackerhausen via Getty Images)

Ultimately, he warned: “Britain, as the latest DWP figures reveal, is now formally moving from guaranteed retirement incomes to incomes based on personal responsibility, but too many people have not adjusted their savings accordingly.

“Yes, we’re in a cost of living crisis and finding any money spare at the end of the month is challenging but people need to have one eye on the future and save as much as they possibly can.

Article continues below

“As people’s retirement incomes become dependent on what they have invested, literally every penny invested into a pension counts.”

News.content:
Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Tuesday as downpours hit 181 regions

It looks set to be a wet couple of days for many Brits, but warmer temperatures should return by the end of this week

View 2 Images The Met Office forecast for 5am on Tuesday (Image: The Met Office)

More than 180 areas could see rain on Tuesday as downpours bring the country’s sunny summer to a temporary halt.

‌



The Met Office is forecasting rainfall in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland across Tuesday, with the vast majority of England also set to see precipitation.

‌



Its forecast, issued at 4am on Monday (August 3), said: “Outbreaks of heavy rain in the north today with a risk of thunder. Scattered showers in the south with the odd thunderstorm. Very warm and humid. Windy in the north.”

‌



However, temperatures will remain high on Tuesday for drier areas, like the south east, where the mercury will reach 28C. Experts also believe a wet couple of days will be followed by more sunshine.

View 2 Images The forecast for midday (Image: The Met Office)

UK weather maps show 7C morning chill with 40 areas below 10C – full list READ MORE :

The Met Office forecast added: “Rather unsettled in the north over the next few days with rain or showers. Some showers in the south at first, but turning drier from Thursday.”

‌



Weather maps show rain will hit 181 council areas across the country, including all 32 in Scotland, all 22 in Wales, and the 11 comprising Northern Ireland.

In England, 116 council areas out of 153 will see some form of rain. The heaviest rain will fall in the afternoon in the north of England, with more than 32mm of precipitation expected in the Yorkshire Dales and in Lancashire.

Heavy rain should also be seen in Cornwall, Devon, Newcastle, and the Scottish Borders on Tuesday evening. Much of the rain comes in the form of a band of cloud moving northeastwards, followed by multiple scattered showers.

‌



Temperatures will remain fairly typical for August. Belfast is expected to see 23C, Cardiff and Manchester 25C, Edinburgh 20C, but London will be warmer with 28C.

News.title: easyJet and British Airways flight warning as Gatwick Airport 'running out of fuel'
News.content:
easyJet and British Airways flight warning as Gatwick Airport 'running out of fuel'

Brits have been warned of disruption at a major UK airport as airlines face the risk of 'running out of fuel' in coming days

View 2 Images Holidaymakers may face disruption due to jet fuel shortages (Image: Getty Images)

Thousands of Brits heading on their summer holidays from a major UK airport could face disruption over the coming days due to a fuel shortage.

‌



Gatwick Airport has sent out a jet fuel warning to pilots as the UK's second-largest airport faces supply issues.

‌



The potential shortage could affect easyJet and British Airways flights from the airport during the peak of the season, as well as other major carriers like Wizz Air, TUI, and Jet2.

‌



View 2 Images The shortage could cause disruption at the airport (Image: Getty Images)

The memo sent out by Gatwick warned airlines: "For the attention of all crews: Gatwick has a shortage of fuel for the next two days.

"Please uplift max possible fuel at outstations."

‌



Another document warned of a "potential disruption to the Gatwick fuel supply".

An airline source told The Sun: "Pilots will try and take on as much fuel as they can from their foreign destinations to bring back to the UK, but they will be limited by factors such as the maximum take-off weight and the maximum landing weight back at Gatwick."

The issue is likely to cause "disruption" from Monday, according to the source.

‌



In the event of an airport fuel infrastructure crisis, major short-haul operators like easyJet can partially insulate themselves by carrying extra fuel from inbound European flights to bypass Gatwick's pumps entirely.

But the airline's sheer flight volume will still put the operation under strain.

Meanwhile, British Airways and other long-haul flight carriers, which cannot tanker fuel and remain entirely dependent on Gatwick's local supply to get off the ground, are more culnerable

‌



It is believed that the shortage is not connected to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, but rather to a technical issue at one of Gatwick's fuel farms.

A spokesperson for Gatwick Airport said: "Following a technical issue impacting fuel supply to the airport, airlines have been advised to monitor fuel availability.

"We are working closely with external suppliers to resolve the issue as quickly as possible and minimise any potential disruption. All airlines are operating as normal."

Article continues below

The Mirror has contacted easyJet and British Airways for further comment.

News.title: Donald Trump claims deal for 'denuclearisation' of Iran will be agreed today
News.content:
Donald Trump claims deal for 'denuclearisation' of Iran will be agreed today

It comes as the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s de facto leader, expressed in a phone call with Trump his concerns about the US potentially escalating the conflict with Iran

View 4 Images Trump gave himself a big pat on the back at the weekend by announcing he had cancelled a planned attack against Iran (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump has claimed a peace deal with Iran is imminent, telling reporters while on board Air Force One on Sunday that the rogue Middle Eastern nation will soon be stripped of all nuclear capabilities. The 47th President of the United States stated that talks between the two warring nations would reconvene on Monday, and the public can to expect to see a deal 'on Hormuz' and 'on the nuclear' very soon. Trump hinted at the incoming peace agreement on Sunday shortly after applauding himself for halting a "massive attack" the US had planned against Iran. In the audio file, the reporter can be heard asking: "What prompted you to call off the strike last night?" To which Trump replied: "I was asked to by Saudi Arabia, by [the] UAE, and by Qatar, and by Iran. We were all set to go, just about at this time right now, and it would have been a massive attack."

‌



View 4 Images US President Donald Trump

‌



The US President continued: "We were all set to go, but when the allies asked to call it off, you gotta sort of say, "Well, let's see." And the reason they asked is I think there's a deal. There's a deal on Hormuz, and then there will be a deal on the nuclear—or, you might call it the denuclearisation of Iran." The suggestion of an actual peace treaty between the US and Iran comes a day or so after Trump took to his preferred social media platform, Truth Social, to give himself a pat himself on the back for not launching further attacks. His post stated: "The U.S.A. is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II.

‌



View 4 Images Donald Trump on the golf course (Image: Getty)

"Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to. This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat. "Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL. "The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment. Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE. Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP."

Article continues below

View 4 Images President Donald Trump meets Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman - a man accused of numerous war crimes and crimes against humanity - at the White House in 2025 (Image: AP)

It comes as Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s de facto leader, expressed in a phone call with Trump his concerns about the US potentially escalating the conflict with Iran, according to a person familiar with the leaders’ discussion. The Saudis, according to the person briefed on the substance of the call but not authorised to comment publicly, are concerned that if the US targets Iran’s energy infrastructure or carries out massive strikes on other key infrastructure that Tehran could respond by carrying out attacks on the kingdom’s and other Gulf countries’ energy infrastructure. The Crown Prince during Saturday’s call sought clarity from Trump on what potential new action he’s weighing to take against Iran, the person said. A White House official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and requested anonymity, confirmed the leaders spoke on Saturday but did not offer any detail about the substance of their conversation.

News.title: How parents and pupils took on 'cruel', 'authoritarian' schools - and won
News.content:
To avoid getting into trouble at school, 14-year-old Amelia says she decided to stop drinking water so she would not need the toilet.

Her school, Camborne Science and International Academy in Cornwall, had introduced strict disciplinary policies, which included limiting toilet visits during classes, according to pupils and former teachers.

New discipline rules were implemented when the school was taken over in January 2024 by the Athena Learning Trust, which runs six secondary schools in Devon and Cornwall.

Amelia's mother, Kayley, believes these strict policies resulted in her daughter becoming ill from a series of serious infections caused by not drinking.

Hundreds of parents, including Kayley, have campaigned against the way Athena run its schools - and their vocal opposition now appears to have paid off. Last month, the trust announced it was planning to disband and transfer all its schools to other trusts.

It said that trustees had "listened carefully to feedback" and recognised the "clear need for change".

BBC Panorama has spoken to nearly 100 pupils, parents and former teachers from Athena schools, who say levels of discipline went too far. Many pupils and parents queued to talk to us at two town hall meetings we arranged.

The way the schools had been run was "authoritarian" and "cruel", some said.

"You're constantly scared you're going to do something wrong," one student with ADHD told us, while a former music teacher said the strict discipline had meant his lessons were taught in silence.

News.title: Woman has pioneering womb surgery to fix 'miracle' baby with intestines outside its body
News.content:
Doctors have used ground-breaking surgery on an unborn baby to successfully correct a birth defect while he was still inside the womb.

His mother, Maisie Savage, from London, was operated on by doctors in the US while she was 26 weeks pregnant.

Baby Theo, who is now five months old and thriving, had gastroschisis, where the belly button does not develop properly, causing the intestines to grow externally.

Doctors partially exposed his mother's womb and then gently pushed his organs back inside his abdomen using keyhole surgery.

He was the third baby in the world to benefit from the first-of-its-kind clinical trial.

News.title: Burnham pledges to be 'relentless' in curbing small boat crossings
News.content:
Andy Burnham has pledged his government will be "relentless" in curbing the number of people arriving in the UK on small boats.

The prime minister said progress had been made and the government was "changing the whole approach", with enforcement officers tackling people-smuggling gangs doubled on both sides of the Channel.

"People want to see this issue addressed," he said in Dover, adding: "We also need to build a system that offers safe routes for people as well, because that also takes away the selling point of the gangs."

The Conservatives said that Labour had not delivered on its promises on migration, while Reform UK said if in government it would deploy the navy to ward off crossings.

Political discussions around the UK's policies on illegal migration have resurfaced since tens of thousands of migrants swam into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on Thursday.

Burnham noted that 98% of the people who swam to the African territory had been returned to Morocco - which he said had dealt with the immediate issue.

But he added: "There's a broader issue about the Schengen area and our relationship with it, and of course, I would want to be in regular dialogue with the EU on those issues."

His comments came shortly after the Home Office announced that the number of National Crime Agency (NCA) officers tackling smuggling gangs facilitating small boat crossings had risen to almost 800 from 376 at the start of 2025.

Burnham said there had been a similar doubling of French officers.

Asked whether he wanted to change the tone of the debate around small boats, he said that he wanted to "deal with the issue rather than play politics with the issue".

He added: "The public don't like the idea that the border looks like it's not controlled. We need to bring back that control. But also we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it."

News.title: Heat health alerts in England as temperatures set to reach 34C
News.content:
Amber and yellow heat health alerts come into effect across much of England on Monday, with temperatures expected to reach 34C in some areas.

The amber alerts, issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), cover London, the South East, the East of England and the East Midlands, from 09:00 BST until the same time on Wednesday 5 August.

The alerts warn that significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures, including a rise in deaths, particularly among vulnerable people.

Less severe yellow heat heat alerts have also been issued for the same period for the North West, Yorkshire and the Humber, West Midlands and the South West.

The North East is currently the only English region without a heat health alert.

The updated warnings replace those issued during last week's heatwave and reflect a fresh spell of potentially hazardous temperatures expected to affect millions across the country.

News.title: What are the 'luteal uglies' and how are they affecting women?
News.content:
"Is it just me or am I the ugliest person alive?" a woman in her early 30s asks the camera on TikTok, accompanied by the caption "POV: Girls in their luteal phase."

The video has 2.4 million views and hundreds of comments.

"This is literally me," one woman writes. "I'm angry at how accurate this is," another says.

There are thousands of videos like this one on social media, lamenting the "luteal uglies" - the changes in appearance and mood that women say appear during the luteal phase of their menstrual cycle.

During this phase, which occurs in the second half of a woman's cycle and ends when she gets her period, women experience a huge drop in oestrogen. So are the "luteal uglies" a real thing?

According to Dr Louise Newson, a GP and women's hormones specialist, this change in hormone levels means women can experience a shift in their appearance, sleep and mood during this time.

"Our hormones affect our skin, they affect our collagen, so a lot of people find their skin becomes drier, their complexion not so bright, they might have acne and spots," Newson explains. "They might get bloating and breasts can change shape."

News.title: Glasgow hailed for saving Games as baton passes to Amdavad
News.content:
The man responsible for delivering Glasgow 2026 said the city had "saved and reinvented" the Commonwealth Games, three years after its future was plunged into doubt.

Ahead of Sunday's closing ceremony - which featured a dazzling fireworks display over the River Clyde - Phil Batty recalled how Glasgow stepped up when the original hosts pulled out.

And he believes the legacy of the sustainable, scaled-back Games will shape the future of the multi-sports event.

The Commonwealth flag was last night ceremonially handed over to the Indian city of Amdavad, which will stage the centenary event in 2030.

But Batty said Glasgow's decision to host the event for a second time in 12 years would never be forgotten.

He told BBC Scotland News: "We have created a Games here that will inspire more nations to host but, probably more importantly, that every nation feels it could host at some point in the next 100 years."

News.title: Almost £200,000 of fuel stolen from UK forecourts every day since Iran war began
News.content:
UK drivers have stolen almost Â£200,000 of fuel from petrol stations on average every day since the Iran war broke out and sent prices soaring, according to industry analysis.

Incidents of fuel being taken from forecourts without payment have risen by a fifth in the five months since 28 February, figures from Forecourt Eye suggest.

The conflict in the Middle East severely disrupted oil supplies across the region, triggering a rise in wholesale prices and subsequent increase in costs at the pump in the UK.

Forecourt Eye said the value of the stolen fuel is estimated to have risen by 48% compared with the five months before the war - to reach an estimated daily average of Â£194,000.

The fuel theft prevention company added petrol stations are reporting an increase in "abuse, intimidation and violence from frustrated customers".

The figures are based on a representative sample of 550 forecourts, comparing the five months prior to the outbreak with the five months after it started, and extrapolated to the UK's 8,359 forecourts.

The number of incidents recorded at the forecourts in the sample equates to 2,872 daily incidents on average at forecourts across the UK in the months after war began, up from around 2,400.

They include people driving off without an attempt to pay, and people claiming they have no way to pay after filling their vehicle.

The volume of stolen fuel rose by 24% - up from an estimated 87,000 litres to 108,900 litres a day across all forecourts.

In response, Forecourt Eye said it would partner with facial recognition company Facewatch to offer more than 2,000 retailers free access to crime reporting technology from the autumn.

News.title: US and Japan take action to prop up yen in rare joint move
News.content:
Japan and the US have confirmed that they jointly intervened last week to halt a slide in the yen after it weakened to a fresh 40-year low.

The joint intervention is the first since 2011, when both countries took coordinated action to weaken the yen after the devastating earthquake and tsunami that hit eastern Japan.

Both Japan's Ministry of Finance and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have said that they will not hesitate to conduct more joint interventions in the future.

It highlights both countries' efforts to prevent a sell-off in the yen and Japanese government bonds from having an impact on the global economy, including potentially helping to push up borrowing costs for Washington.

"The United States agreed to participate in the coordinated intervention because it serves its national interests by offering the prospect of significant benefits at a low cost," Shigeto Nagai, head of Japan economics at Oxford Economics told the BBC.

The two countries are expected to continue to intervene "intermittently in a coordinated manner for some time", he added.

"Even if the actual amount of intervention is not particularly large, the prolonged sense of vigilance regarding intervention will be effective in deterring speculators."

The yen is historically weak mainly due to Japan having much lower central bank interest rates than other major economies like the US. That makes the Japanese currency less attractive to international investors.

The Bank of Japan last raised interest rates in June, as it increased its main rate to 1% - the highest level since September 1995. In comparison, the US Federal Reserve's benchmark rate is in a range of 3.50% to 3.75%.

Japan also faces other issues including a decades-long slide in its working-age population, low productivity and a heavy reliance on energy imports that are priced in US dollars.

On Monday, Japan's finance ministry said Friday's intervention with the US Treasury Department "countered excessive volatility and disorderly movements in the Japanese yen in recent months".

The "coordinated foreign exchange actions countered disorderly yen movements," Bessent said in a social media post.

"We strongly support Japan's decisive market and monetary steps to correct the substantial undervaluation of the yen," he added.

"They have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we're always there for Japan," US President Donald Trump told reporters on Sunday.

News.title: At least five Al Fayed survivors confirmed as modern slavery victims
News.content:
At least five women who were abused by former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed have been formally recognised by the Home Office as victims of modern slavery.

The BBC revealed in April that Rachel Louw, who has waived her right to anonymity, had become the first woman known to receive such a decision.

Since then, at least four other women have received positive "conclusive grounds" decisions recognising them as victims of modern slavery, with more expected to follow, according to PA Media.

The latest cases include women who were trafficked internationally and within the UK, including one case in which the trafficking took place entirely within Harrods.

When an individual receives a positive "conclusive grounds" decision through the National Referral Mechanism (NRM) - the UK's official framework for identifying victims of modern slavery - they are formally recognised as a victim.

Legal experts have previously told the BBC that these decisions can strengthen the credibility of witnesses in criminal proceedings and may influence the way police investigate cases.

The Modern Slavery Act, which came into force in 2015, defines human trafficking as arranging or facilitating the travel of another person within a country or across borders for the purposes of that person being exploited.

The latest decisions include all four members of the survivor advocacy group No One Above, who had been awaiting rulings after being referred to the NRM by the anti-slavery charity Unseen.

According to PA Media, one survivor had been recruited to a false role within Harrods, while two others were employed in legitimate roles before being selected for abuse from the shop floor.

A fourth worked as a domestic employee for the Fayed family after being recruited by a letting agency called Hyde Park Residence.

One of the survivors said receiving the decision was "very significant".

"Seeing it in writing that you were a victim of modern slavery and trafficking is very... it's really shocking to read," she told PA Media.

News.title: Man admits transporting Scottish woman's body in suitcase, Greek police say
News.content:
Greek police say a man has admitted transporting the body of a Scottish woman in a suitcase to an abandoned building.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July, days after she was reported missing.

Local officers launched an investigation with cooperation from authorities in the US, the UK and Scotland, and now say they have arrested a 26-year-old man - the BBC understands he is from Afghanistan.

The force said he was brought to police headquarters on Thursday where he "confessed to his actions". He was arrested on suspicion of manslaughter, robbery and weapons offences, but the exact charges have yet to be finalised under the Greek legal system.

News.title: Prolonged drought could cause shortage of some foods, farmers' union head says
News.content:
Bradshaw also suggested farmers should be given tax breaks to build water storage systems on their land to prepare for the years ahead.

"We have taken our food supply for granted for far too long," he added.

"Those other countries around the world that we currently rely on to produce our food and vegetables, their climates are changing as well.

"It does feel like there is going be some shortages of [food] products", Bradshaw told Radio 4's Broadcasting House.

In a message to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, he said: "Let's draw a line in the sand and make sure we prioritise domestic food production to deliver growth across the UK."

After a wet and mild start to the year, it has been exceptionally dry hot and dry with a succession of heatwaves across the UK.

The combination of low rainfall and prolonged heat has quickly depleted water reserves in soils, vegetation and rivers.

While droughts can occur naturally, climate change is making weather patterns more erratic, and heatwaves more frequent and intense.

Scientists say there is a greater risk of droughts happening as a result, and of them being more severe and longer-lasting when they do.

The Met Office reports that England saw just 5.6mm of rainfall up to 30 July â just 8% of its long-term meteorological average for the month and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.

For Wales it was 7.9mm of rainfall, also 8% of its long-term average for the month and almost a third of the previous record of 22.6mm, again set in 1911.

Heat health alerts are in place across most of England until at least 09:00 BST on Wednesday.

Amber alerts indicate a rise in deaths of vulnerable people and increased demand on health services are likely, while yellow alerts indicate these are possible.

News.title: Ballot paper for Clacton by-election is longest in British electoral history
News.content:
The longest ballot paper in British political history is costing four times as much to print than regular ballot papers, the local council has said.

The list for the Clacton parliamentary by-election, which was prompted by the resignation of Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, is 90cm (3ft) long.

When people unfold the paper, they will find it is longer than most adults' arms.

Tendring District Council chief executive Ian Davidson - who is the acting returning officer for the by-election in the Essex constituency - said organising the vote had been "manic".

People have already started returning postal votes to town hall and most registered voters will go to polling stations on 13 August.

Davidson said: "We've logistically been looking at the size of the ballot paper, how we fold it to get it into the envelope so we can send it out to our postal voters [and] how we manage the polling stations."

News.title: Teenager dies after 'medical episode' at Kendal Calling festival in Cumbria
News.content:
A teenage girl died at the Kendal Calling festival in the early hours of the morning, police have said.

The 17-year-old suffered a medical episode at about 02:15 BST and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to Cumbria Police. The force asked people not to speculate about the circumstances of the incident.

It added officers were looking into the circumstances and wanted to speak to anyone who was in the area of the Calling Out tent and the Big Wheel around the time of the girl's death.

A spokesperson said: "Officers are particularly keen to speak with a group of women who alerted first responders to the girl after becoming concerned for her welfare."

They said the girl's family had been informed and were being supported by specialist officers.

The force asked people not to speculate, saying it could have a "significant impact" on the family and friends involved.

"We would ask that the investigation be allowed to take its course."

News.title: Three in hospital after fire and crush at festival in London
News.content:
Three people were taken to hospital after a fire and crush at the entrance of a festival.

Organisers of Ghana Party in the Park, also known as Shattafest UK, at Copthall Playing Fields in Barnet, London, said the event was stopped following a "major incident" at about 18:00 BST on Saturday.

The Metropolitan Police said a fire had started near the gates, which meant they were closed temporarily.

A crowd built up, and there was a surge when the gates reopened, it said.

Organisers said the decision to end the festival was made on health and safety grounds.

They said in a statement the day had been "one of the most difficult" in the event's history and called what happened "deeply upsetting".

News.title: Aerial footage shows wildfire tearing through Suffolk heathland
News.content:
The Suffolk wildfire has grown to an area equal to more than 200 football pitches, Suffolk's fire service says.

The wildfire broke out on Dunwich Heath in Suffolk on Wednesday, with a major incident declared due to its "size and complexity".

Read more about the wildfire here.

News.title: My dog Axel 'wouldn't get on' with Larry the cat, says Burnham
News.content:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Laura Kuenssberg his dog Axel will be staying in Greater Manchester and will not be moving to No 10 Downing Street.

Burnham revealed he does not think his poodle-mix would get along with Larry the cat, who has lived at the residence for 15 years.

Watch Panorama Andy Burnham: The Laura Kuenssberg Interview on iPlayer from 06:00BST, and on BBC One at 20:00BST on Mon 27 Jul 2026.

The Universities of Kent and Greenwich have merged to create what they describe as the UK’s first ”super-university”.

The new London and South East University Group, to be known as LASE, has more than 50,000 students and four campuses across London, Medway and Kent, and has become the third largest university in the UK.

The two universities will still operate as distinct academic divisions within the university group, retaining their current names.

Students will still apply to and graduate from the institution that they pick.

The higher education institutions announced plans to merge in September last year. The official launch will take place on 7 September, exactly one year on.

The University of Greenwich and the University of Kent have merged to become the UK’s first ‘super-university’ ( University of Greenwich/PA )

It comes as universities in the UK have been facing increasing financial pressures, with MPs on the Education Committee warning earlier this year that there is a “real risk” a university in England could close due to insolvency for the first time.

The Office for Students (OfS), the higher education regulator in England, told the committee that it fears 24 providers are at risk of becoming insolvent and closing in the 12 months from November last year, and warned 45 per cent of higher education providers could be facing a deficit for 2025/26.

The universities of Greenwich and Kent said previously that their merged group will provide a strong financial foundation for getting through economic challenges and would be a “blueprint for others to follow”.

In May, King’s College London and Cranfield University, based in Bedford, announced plans to merge in August 2027.

University of Greenwich vice-chancellor and new chief executive of LASE Professor Jane Harrington said: “There has been tireless work over the last year working to an ambitious timetable and developing a new university model that has never been done before.

“It means we are starting with a smooth transition, an extremely strong senior executive team and clear direction so that we can fulfil our potential as the UK’s first super-university.”

News.title: Newcastle are at a crossroads – can little-known manager Matthias Jaissle find a new way?
News.content:
