World.title: How Trans-Caspian Cable Fits Kazakhstan’s Evolving Connectivity Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA — For decades, Kazakhstan’s connectivity strategy was measured in highways, railways and pipelines. Today, that vision is expanding. As global competition increasingly depends on the movement of data alongside the movement of goods, the country is investing in a new layer of strategic infrastructure — one designed not to carry cargo, but information.

Among the clearest examples of this shift is the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable project. The first-ever underwater telecommunications link across the Caspian Sea will connect Aktau and Sumqayit, creating a new digital corridor between Central Asia, the South Caucasus and Europe.

The project reflects a broader vision articulated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who has increasingly framed Kazakhstan’s connectivity agenda as extending beyond physical transport routes to include cross-border digital infrastructure. In his September 2024 State of the Nation Address, he called for the project to be completed, describing it as essential for “creating a digital infrastructure linked with international corridors and cross-border data flows.”

Several months later, speaking at an informal meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Organization of Turkic States in Budapest, Tokayev expanded that vision beyond Kazakhstan.

“This project will significantly improve digital communication between our countries and will be a strategic step towards strengthening regional integration. Such initiatives open up opportunities to create a new digital corridor across the Eurasian continent,” he said.

The regional context continues to evolve. As the cable enters its final construction phase, regional leaders are once again gathering, this time in Cholpon-Ata for an informal Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, underscoring how cooperation between the countries increasingly extends across transport, energy and digital connectivity.

Nearly two years after Tokayev first identified the project as a strategic priority, it is entering its most tangible phase. Kazakhstan is now carrying out the final stages of the project, with commercial commissioning expected by the end of 2026. The latest phase has shifted from engineering preparation to offshore construction.

According to the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development’s release from July 31, regulatory, customs and organizational procedures have been completed, including the approval of equipment required for the offshore works, allowing construction to proceed without administrative delays.

Preparatory work in 2025 included desktop and offshore engineering surveys, selection of the optimal route avoiding anchorage zones and military training areas, environmental approvals from the Mangystau Region authorities, and the production and factory testing in China of a specially armored submarine cable equipped with ROPA optical amplifiers.

With the planning phase complete, attention has shifted from engineering design to execution at sea. The cable, previously delivered from China to the port of Kuryk together with three cable baskets weighing a combined 600 tons, was transported to Baku aboard a specialized logistics vessel. It has now been transferred into the cable tank of the cable-laying vessel, which has departed Baku and is laying the line toward Aktau.

The operation is being carried out by a cable-laying vessel with a displacement exceeding 20,000 tons and equipped with dynamic positioning technology to ensure precise installation on the seabed. Around 70 crew members are involved, including technical supervisors and representatives of Kazakhtelecom. The project is being implemented by CaspiLink B.V., the joint venture established by Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom.

A dedicated jointing room has also been installed onboard to allow engineers to repair or reconnect the cable if required during installation. Both the Kazakh and Azerbaijani cable ends have already undergone testing. Subject to favorable weather conditions, installation of the submarine cable is expected to be completed within the next 15 to 20 days, while the overall commissioning process remains on schedule for completion by the end of 2026.

The significance of the project, however, extends well beyond the technical operation. As economies become more deeply integrated through both physical and digital infrastructure, international corridors are no longer defined solely by the goods they carry. They are increasingly shaped by the data they enable to move across borders. While the cable spans just 380 kilometers across the Caspian seabed, the vision behind it reaches much further. The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable reflects Kazakhstan’s ambition to remain an important link in the movement of both goods and data across Eurasia.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Daughter laments 'indescribable' absence six months after mother vanished
World.content:
The daughter of a woman who disappeared in northern NSW nearly six months ago has described the pain of living without answers.

Yvonne Whear, 73, was last seen was on the afternoon of February 19, when her car was recorded on CCTV travelling along Queensland Road in the direction of her farm near Murwillumbah.

"I just can't believe that six months has almost gone by," her daughter Gillian Hallac said.

"I haven't been able to sleep; we just can't do anything.

" It's just indescribable because she's there one day and all of a sudden there's no her, there's no car, there's nothing, there's no answers. "

Gillian Hallac is joining NSW Police to appeal for information about the disappearance of her mother Yvonne Whear. (ABC News)

Ms Hallac said her mother had been to an art class at TAFE on the day of her disappearance.

She was seen at the Shell service station on Tweed Valley Way at Murwillumbah about 3:15pm.

Evidence suggests she made it home: the boots and hat she was wearing were found there.

Phone records also show Ms Whear watched some videos and shortly before 5pm, checked her voicemail.

She has not been seen or heard from since and her car has never been found.

Yvonne Whear was last seen driving her car on February 19. It has never been found. (Supplied: Facebook)

A plea for answers

Ms Hallac said her mother might have been taken from the property and her vehicle deliberately concealed.

"That is my belief as her daughter, based on what I know about the circumstances in which she disappeared," she said.

"I strongly believe that there are people out there who know more than what they have been saying."

Yvonne Whear had attended a TAFE art class on the day of her disappearance. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Ms Hallac said her mother was a "very private" person who cared deeply for the animals she kept on her small farm, and spoke to her family "almost every day".

"Since mum disappeared, she has missed countless family occasions," Ms Hallac said.

"Most painfully, she missed meeting her first great-grandchild.

"We need to know where she is and what happened to her. We miss her presence in our lives every day."

Police open to all possibilities

Detective Inspector Paul Fenwick, the manager of the NSW Police missing persons registry, said "significant resources" had been invested into the search for Ms Whear.

"[Police have used] drones and helicopters that have travelled as far north from Murwillumbah up to Tomewin, which is just near the Queensland border," he said.

"Police boats and police divers, using sonar equipment, have travelled through the Rous and the Tweed Rivers as far east as Fingal Head."

NSW Police said Ms Whear's disappearance was the subject of "considerable speculation" but the investigation remained open to all possibilities.

Inspector Fenwick said there was no evidence to suggest Ms Whear intended to voluntarily disappear.

Yvonne Whear's disappearance has been the subject of a widespread appeal for help and "considerable speculation". (Supplied)

"We're asking [for people to come forward] if anyone had seen Yvonne, if anyone had seen her car, if anyone had been through that area that time and was capturing dash cam footage that hadn't been reviewed at all, if they saw anything unusual at all … regardless of how small they feel it is," he said.

The appeal comes during National Missing Persons Week, which aims to raise public awareness about cases across the country.

Inspector Fenwick said it was important to acknowledge the uncertainty families faced.

"Although time passes, the need for answers never does," he said.

"Our theme this year is simple but strong: that answers still matter."

World.title: Height limit for new Canberra precinct reduced after community outcry
World.content:
The federal government has approved an amendment which will pave the way for the redevelopment of an area in Canberra's inner-south, despite some community opposition.

Minister for Regional Development, Local Government and Territories Kristy McBain has signed off on changes to the National Capital Plan, which will allow for increased housing in the area of Hume Circle, close to Griffith and Narrabundah.

However, the National Capital Authority (NCA), who is responsible for the redevelopment, has bowed to community calls to significantly reduce proposed building height limits after facing opposition from locals worried about traffic and overshadowing.

It says the design it has landed on is based on the original vision of Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, and is an opportunity to "revitalise, embed design excellence, and celebrate Canberra's unique landscape character".

Changes made to retain 'character'

In response to community feedback, the maximum allowable building height has been reduced in several sections of Hume Circle, including to three storeys in a southern section of the circle.

A map indicating building height limits within the Hume Circle Precinct in Canberra's inner-south. (Supplied: National Capital Authority)

Further planning and design work is expected and will need to be submitted for NCA approval and public consultation before it can proceed to construction.

But NCA chief executive Karen Doran said they had made changes to the plan to "make sure that the precinct code was clear on what was expected in those areas to preserve their existing character".

"So building height there, for instance in an existing low-rise residential area, was brought down to three storeys which is the current height in that area," Ms Doran said.

"It sends the message that part of the precinct is intended to retain its character and existing use.

"In other areas of the precinct, [like] the industrial area which is on the eastern side of the precinct, the heights there have also been reduced from the 15 storeys down to a maximum of 12 storeys, and eight storeys in other sections."

National Capital Authority chief executive Karen Doran said community feedback on the Hume Circle Precinct had been incorporated into the amendment. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Residents who opposed the plans due to the proposed building heights say they are still concerned about the redevelopment, despite the reduction to three storeys for their particular neighbourhood.

Ludmilla Milo lives on Staffordshire Terrace, which is just a few hundred metres from Hume Circle.

"Changing the planning permissions to keep this as three storeys, well that's a small win for us," she said.

"But ... there's no guarantees. Down the track ... it could be a landmark 15-storey development here.

" I'm an outright owner, I've set myself up for my future, and it's all in limbo now. "

Ludmilla Milo owns an apartment on Staffordshire Terrace in Canberra's inner-south. (ABC News: Harry Frost)

Traffic, overshadowing concerns addressed

Residents had also previously aired concerns about the impact of the development on the aspect at their properties, which Ms Doran said had been considered in the updated plan.

"It covers off the issues of solar access overshadowing, not only where the development is happening but in the surrounding areas as well," she said.

Ms Doran said further feedback from those worried the development would cause traffic congestion had also been heard, observing that it would be installed "close to public transport and close to employment".

"But we acknowledge that increased housing supply also brings the need to look at continuing the ... provision of suitable infrastructure for people in that precinct," she said.

Draft plan to transform Canberra's 'bleak motorways' released The plan is for mid-rise housing to be developed closest to transport stops and shopping centres, with high-rise development reserved for the Woden Town Centre and north Curtin.

"So one of the initiatives we have set up is a ... governance steering committee to oversight the potential development in the Hume Circle precinct.

"That will bring NCA and ACT government representatives to the table and ensure a coordinated and an integrated approach to development in the precinct."

Federal government taking on responsibility

The changes to the National Capital Plan mean some residential areas will now fall under the NCA's control, rather than ACT government's.

Extending the Hume Circle precinct to McMillan Crescent — and thereby taking in streets such as Staffordshire Terrace — is a key part of the plan.

"The junctions between the main avenues were planned to be important gateways to the National Capital marked by elegant nodes framed by mixed land use and urban form," the amendment says.

"The Griffins' plans for Canberra envisaged the main avenues and approach routes as axial lines and principal ordering elements of the city.

"A new shared way through Sub-Precinct C completes the Griffin geometry of the Outer Circle of McMillan Crescent.

" The shared way will be primarily pedestrian in nature, with limited vehicle use accommodated within low-speed shared zones. "

Map showing the area of the proposed Hume Circle precinct in Canberra's inner-south that is covered by amendments to the National Capital Plan. (Supplied: National Capital Authority)

But Kevin Gibbs, who has lived on Staffordshire Terrace for more than 20 years, said he was worried the NCA wanted to "take control of our apartments".

"We want to be taken out of the National Capital Authority Plan," he said.

"They can have the Hume Circle over the other side, but we're existing residential.

" We'll be paying our rates to the ACT government but we'll be under the planning control of the NCA, where we have really limited come-back if they decide to change what they want to do within this precinct. "

Ms Milo added that the approval was "not the news we wanted to hear today, that we're under NCA control now".

'Who's going to buy?

Mr Gibbs said another concern among residents was that, should they want to sell their property, they would have to reveal to potential buyers the oversight of the NCA.

He said he was also concerned about the word "should" appearing in the amendment documents, which he had interpreted to mean building heights could still be raised in the future.

"It's written there that they at any stage can change [the limit] to 15 or 12 storeys," he said.

"Who's going to buy?"

Staffordshire Terrace resident Kevin Gibbs is against plans for redevelopment in his area of Canberra. (ABC News: Harry Frost)

But Ms Doran said those fears were unfounded.

"What's now in the National Capital Plan is legislation, and so any amendment of that requires the full process of a legislative change, approval by our minister and the government as well as agreement through ACT government," she said.

"The legislation codifies the existing form of development in that area and so it doesn't enable changes to the land use or the building height in that area.

"We are hoping that that gives them comfort as to uncertainty as to preserving the character and the nature of their existing homes."

'We need to plan for liveability'

Earlier this year, a petition against the plans put to the ACT Legislative Assembly and sponsored by independent MLA Thomas Emerson attracted more than 600 signatures.

Today Mr Emerson said a "range of outstanding concerns still need to be addressed".

He is backing calls for the development application to be referred to an inquiry by the Joint Standing Committee on the National Capital and External Territories.

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson is a critic of the NCA's proposal. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"If we're serious about doing density well in Canberra, we need to plan for liveability at the outset," he said in a statement.

"That should include clearly mapping out community infrastructure like active travel connections, playgrounds, schools and early learning centres, shared green spaces and other local neighbourhood amenities.

"There should be adequate representation of all impacted parties, including residents, in the working group tasked with progressing this proposal."

Federal ACT Senator David Pocock also called for an inquiry.

"I would also urge the National Capital Authority to ensure there is appropriate community representation on the proposed working group," Mr Pocock said.

He said he had contacted Ms McBain earlier in the year to make a range of requests which have since been ignored.

These requests included indications of what the urban structure, pedestrian connections and landscape structure would look like as a result of the redevelopment, as well as an overshadowing analysis and preliminary traffic studies.

World.title: Liberty Bell Bay smelter officially enters liquidation
World.content:
Attempts will soon begin to claw back tens of millions of dollars owed to creditors by Australia's only manganese alloy smelter after creditors voted to liquidate Liberty Bell Bay.

At a meeting this afternoon, creditors appointed former administrators, EY Parthenon, as liquidators.

The 66-year-old smelter in northern Tasmania went into administration in March, due to longstanding issues with former owner GFG Alliance.

After a potential sale collapsed last month, it officially closed, leaving 200 workers without jobs.

Liberty Bell Bay smelter workers had been hoping a buyer could be found. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

A recent report to creditors found it may have been trading while insolvent for almost a year and is understood to owe creditors between $70 million and $300 million, including $27 million to workers.

With the company now in liquidation, workers can apply to the federal government's Fair Entitlements Guarantee for many of their entitlements, including unpaid wages, redundancy pay, annual leave and long service leave.

FEG payments are capped at the maximum weekly wage of $3,032.

It does not cover unpaid superannuation.

"We encourage all impacted workers and their families to engage with the dedicated webpage set up by the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, which provides clear information on supports and entitlements," a Commonwealth government spokesperson said.

Affected workers can access the webpage here.

Government focused on 'best possible outcome'

In a statement, Minister for Business, Industry and Resources, Felix Ellis, said the decision to place Liberty Bell Bay into liquidation was "deeply disappointing for the communities of George Town, Bell Bay and Northern Tasmania".

"The Tasmanian government remains focused on ensuring workers and their families are supported during this time.

"Liquidation does not diminish the strategic potential of the site. There is third-party interest, and the government will engage constructively with the liquidator and prospective proponents as opportunities for its future are explored.

"The Tasmanian government is backing the region, with its Northern Economic Plan to be released at the end of August."

World.title: Coal miner dies after 'mobile equipment incident' in NSW Hunter Valley
World.content:
A mine worker has died at a coal mine in the NSW Upper Hunter.

The fatality occurred at the United Wambo Open Cut mine, 16 kilometres west of Singleton.

The mine is a joint venture between mining companies Glencore and Peabody.

Glencore confirmed a worker had died following a "mobile equipment incident" at the mine.

In a statement, CEO Peter Sharpe said it was "tragic news".

"Our sincere condolences go out to the worker's family, friends and colleagues," he said.

"Our immediate focus is on providing support to the worker's family and our employees."

Glencore said emergency services and police were on site, and mining operations were being suspended.

The Mining and Energy Union's Northern Mining and NSW Energy District president Robin Williams said the union was sending condolences to the worker's loved ones.

"Every worker has the right to come home safely at the end of every shift," he said.

"Any workplace fatality is one too many.

"Right now, the focus needs to be on supporting the workforce and respecting the privacy of the family."

Mr Williams said a union safety officer was on site investigating.

"It's important the relevant authorities are given the time and space to conduct a thorough investigation so the circumstances of this tragedy can be fully understood," he said.

World.title: Cable Beach camel bucks tourists off during sunset ride
World.content:
Two people were bucked off one of Broome's camels during a ride on Cable Beach, in Western Australia's far north, over the weekend.

Footage shows two people trying to hold onto the camel on Saturday evening after the spooked animal broke away from the rest of the group.

The couple are flung from the camel and hit the hard sand, as it continues to buck up and down.

A St John Ambulance spokesperson said paramedics took a woman in her 60s to Broome Hospital, under priority two conditions, which indicates a serious injury.

WA Country Health confirmed one person had been discharged from Broome Hospital, while another person was in a stable condition.

Camel rides are popular on Broome's Cable Beach. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

It was not known what caused the camel to go rogue and break away from the group.

Camel rides on the picturesque Cable Beach attract tens of thousands of tourists every year.

Considered a quintessential part of a Broome holiday for many, the camel rides have been operating since the 1980s.

It is understood two tourists involved in the incident were part of a larger travelling group.

Shire of Broome president Chris Mitchell said such incidents were uncommon.

Chris Mitchell says his thoughts are with the family of those injured. (ABC Kimberley: Andy Seabourne)

"Our thoughts are with those injured in the incident, and we wish them a speedy recovery," he said.

"Camel tours are a longstanding and much-loved part of the Broome experience, and incidents like this are rare.

"Broome continues to be a safe and welcoming destination, offering unique experiences enjoyed by thousands of visitors each year."

A representative from tour company Red Sun Camels said they were unable to comment.

World.title: Now bird flu has hit seagulls a 'super-spreader' event is more likely
World.content:
It's hard not to think of Australia's hotel quarantine system during the COVID-19 pandemic while waiting to see what would happen with the animal equivalent, a global bird flu panzootic, on our shores.

In the early stages of the COVID response we were given the daily numbers of returning Australians testing positive to the virus. All the while we held our breath waiting to see if it would spread out into the wider community.

It's been a similar feeling as migratory birds from Antarctic waters started washing up in mid-June with the H5N1 avian influenza that has swept the globe killing millions of animals.

Infected giant petrels and a brown skua, that travel seasonally to chill in the ocean off Australia in winter, were kept in vet clinics as we kept our fingers crossed there would be no local spread.

But now the humble seagull getting H5N1, coupled with a mass mortality of greater crested terns, marks a new stage for bird flu's spread in Australia.

Until the first seagull was detected with H5 in South Australia last week, the only birds with the virus were terns and those migratory seabirds which stick to the ocean or beaches.

But seagulls, the common name for the silver gull species, can move vast distances around the country taking advantage of resources be it nicking chips or hanging out at tips.

Potential for long-distance spread

Seagulls can be found nearly everywhere in Australia, from beaches to cities, freshwater systems, mountains and landfills. They even pop up in the middle of the country when big rains fill up sites like Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre.

This lifestyle gives them the potential to act as a crossover species in spreading the virus to a range of different environments and other bird species.

"They're more cosmopolitan in their requirements, [eating at] tips, shopping alleys," Chris Purnell, the wetland and migratory shorebirds manager at Birdlife Australia, told me.

" They'll mingle with everything and often parasitise [steal from] other birds and eat their eggs. "

Seagulls also poo in a lot of places, which is one of the big ways the virus spreads.

They spend a lot of time around greater crested terns, which have tested positive to H5N1 in SA and Victoria so far, mixing together in large groups.

Both species are coming into their nesting seasons where they can form colonies of thousands.

Silver gulls in South Australia nest between June and December with the exact timing varying colony to colony.

Silver gulls and greater crested terns often mingle on beaches around Australia. (iNaturalist: Tim, Great crested tern, CC BY 4.0)

To borrow a term from the COVID-19 pandemic, those are potential super-spreader events.

And they are a real concern when this particular type of H5N1, the clade 2.3.4.4b, wiped out millions of wild and domestic birds and thousands of seals around the world in just a few years, including gulls.

The black-headed gull, a close relative of the silver gull, has been the subject of mass die-offs in Europe from this type of H5N1, with an estimated 51,000 adult birds dying in 2023 in Poland.

Mass bird deaths are a live concern given what has happened elsewhere in the world and with the first Australian mass mortality of 49 dead greater crested terns over the weekend in SA.

Australian Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson said on Monday it had taken a little longer than expected to see a localised spread occurring since the first migratory bird detections.

"Now that we have got that localised spread, this is following a fairly predictable curve in terms of the number of infections," she said.

"Particularly during a period of year as we might start to see birds start to congregate more.

"We know when birds and other animals congregate that's where we get more risk of circulation of the virus and onward spread."

H5N1 here to stay

Technical advice last week to the federal government puts Australia past the point where the virus may have been eradicated, particularly with a local spread occurring in SA.

Skye Fruean, the chief veterinary officer of South Australia, said the disease was here to stay.

"Once we started to get that really strong evidence of that transmission between the crested terns, that does change things in terms of our decision making."

Loading

Dr Fruean told SA Country Hour on Friday that surveillance was still the primary focus but state and federal governments were looking now at what else they should be doing in terms of virus management.

That includes discussions around what should trigger a mandatory housing order for free-range chicken operations.

"At this point in time it is an option open to jurisdictions," Dr Fruean said.

Bringing chickens indoors keeps them away from the potential exposure to water contaminated by wild infected birds and the latter's faeces.

That's because chickens are highly susceptible to this strain and more than 100 million have died or been culled in the US since its first outbreak in 2022.

But it's still early days yet, with states weighing up the risks and whether chickens need to be locked down.

Duck, duck, virus

The biggest turning point for different states could be when the virus shows up in water fowl like wild ducks.

Ducks are thought to have co-evolved with bird flu viruses like H5 as they can be silent spreaders showing little signs of illness.

The virus also spreads rapidly among ducks as it can survive for multiple days within freshwater bodies that ducks both defecate in and eat from.

It's not out of the realms of possibility that a bird such as a seagull or a pelican could now be the bridging species that takes the virus from the coast and brings it to ducks.

When I rang Dr Purnell on Friday he was visiting Victoria's volcanic lake system, west of Melbourne, where seagulls were starting to gather for nesting.

Ducks and other freshwater birds are also highly mobile and move between major water systems.

So, the virus has the potential to move big distances and make its way around the country from a single incursion.

Past tracking studies of species like ibis and spoonbill, for instance, on the east coast of Australia show a 2,000 kilometre flyway over the Murray Darling Basin. Individual birds were tracked flying all along the system and up to northern Queensland.

With the local spread of the virus in SA, there are major areas of concern for initial outbreaks in internationally significant wetlands like the Coorong at the mouth of the Murray River.

The Coorong is home to more than 200 bird species, and is a major stopover for millions of migratory shorebirds which start arriving in September from the northern hemisphere each year. They too will be vulnerable to the virus.

While we can't predict what exactly will happen from now with the virus's spread, any wishful thinking it wouldn't establish in local birds is past.

And as federal agriculture minister Julie Collins said on Monday, we should expect to see an increase in the number of birds getting H5N1 in Australia.

"Sadly, we do know that once the H5 bird flu is spreading in wildlife and the natural environment, it is not possible to avoid significant losses, which is what we are starting to see now," she said.

"Australians should expect to see more [H5] spread and larger numbers now of wildlife being affected."

Anyone who sees a dead or sick bird is asked not to touch it and report it to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888.

World.title: RFK Jr urges parents to vaccinate kids amid record measles outbreak
World.content:
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has urged parents to vaccinate their children following a record-breaking measles outbreak in the United States.

Mr Kennedy, a longtime vaccine critic who has regularly told Americans they should not take medical advice from him, warned people to get the jab during a heated interview on CNN on Sunday, local time.

“Parents should get their children vaccinated for measles," he said.

"A measles vaccine is effective, it stops measles in about 97 per cent of the cases. People should get vaccinated.”

The rise in measles, declared essentially eradicated in the US a quarter of a century ago, has been linked by medical experts to slumping immunisation rates, a trend many attribute in part to vaccine scepticism espoused by Mr Kennedy.

More than 2,370 cases of measles have been confirmed in the US this year, already breaking last year's multi-decade high.

RFK Jr defended his handling of the measles outbreak in the interview with Dana Bash. (Supplied)

During the CNN interview, Mr Kennedy was asked if he took any responsibility for the measles surge.

“Absolutely not,” he said.

Mr Kennedy later went on to accuse CNN host Dana Bash of "repeating like a parrot" and becoming "flustered".

Worst year for measles in decades

Many health officials have cited a public backlash to the government's pandemic response and blame Mr Kennedy's anti-vaccine policies for further undermining trust in immunisations.

Measles outbreak in US prompts questions over RFK Jr's vaccination messages Under the watch of Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr a vaccine-preventable disease has continued to spread across the US.

"The whole thing about 'vaccines have been tested and there's been this determination made' is just a lie," Mr Kennedy said in a 2025 interview.

The nation had 2,289 cases in 2025, the most since 1991.

This year there have been major outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah and Arizona, as well as smaller clusters in other states.

International health officials will meet in November to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.

The US eliminated the local spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but in recent years they have fallen below the 95 per cent coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.

Measles cases under-counted

Public health departments and disease researchers have long acknowledged that official counts of disease cases are incomplete because not everyone seeks treatment.

Measles testing was conducted in Texas in 2025 (Reuters: Sebastian Rocandio)

Experts suspect the spread of measles cases may be wider than has been reported due to the decline in vaccination rates.

National vaccination rates for measles, mumps and rubella — which dropped to 92.5 per cent among kindergarteners in the 2024-25 school year, from 95.2 per cent in 2019-20 — obscure even lower rates in certain communities.

In Utah, where public health officials have fought measles for more than a year, the virus has struck more than 700 people during that time, according to the state health department.

Experts relying on mathematical modelling and genetic analyses indicate that a large outbreak on the Utah-Arizona border could be three to four times bigger than what is known, according to Utah state epidemiologist Leisha Nolen.

ABC/wires

World.title: Tasmania free from bird flu, but experts say a case of when, not if
World.content:
Tasmania is waiting for a deadly strain of bird flu to reach its shores as cases spread on the mainland and authorities warn it is not a matter of if, but when.

H5 bird flu has spread across the globe, killing millions of wild birds, tens of thousands of wild mammals and devastating poultry industries.

Since arriving in Western Australia in June, it has shown up in wild seabirds in all jurisdictions except for Tasmania, the Northern Territory and the Australian Capital Territory.

Bird flu risks While birds are the most likely victims of the deadly strain of bird flu that has just reached our shores, researchers are also sounding the alarm for our native marsupial species.

Australia has now confirmed its first mass mortality in greater crested terns at Baudin Rocks, off Cape Jaffa in South Australia.

Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said while not unexpected, it was a disappointing development.

"Sadly, we do know that once the H5 bird flu is spreading in wildlife and the natural environment, it is not possible to avoid significant losses, which is what we're starting to see now," she said.

As the interstate tally grows, Tasmania's Chief Veterinary Officer Deborah McSweyn said the probability of arrival increased.

"It is not possible to prevent it from coming to Tasmania as it will be carried here in wild birds," she said.

Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania secretary Jason Jacobi said an incident management team had been working "around the clock" to prepare.

"We all need to remain calm, our response needs to be measured, we cannot afford to catastrophise this, but we all need to be ready for the fact that it will be hard," he told 936 ABC Radio Hobart.

" No-one wants to see sick or dying wild birds or marine mammals. "

Where exactly the bird flu will hit first remains in question, but Mr Jacobi suspected it would be along the coast.

"These are typically going to be birds like crested terns, giant petrels, brown skuas that have come in from remote coastal islands, so it's likely that they will arrive on the beaches, but they could turn up anywhere," he said.

Loading...

The incident management team has been patrolling beaches, including at King Island and the Furneaux Islands.

"We've now stood up a four-week program of drone surveillance of all of our coastline, and that is also being supported by on-ground land-based patrolling," Mr Jacobi said.

But authorities stressed efforts relied on the reporting of sick or dead birds.

"Avoid any contact, stay well away from the bird and keep your pets well away," he said.

"Use your phone or any other mechanism you've got to record the condition of the bird and its location; we need to know where it is, we need to be able to identify what species of wild bird or wild animal it might be, and then report it."

Dr McSweyn said symptoms included swimming in circles, coughing and sneezing, an inability to stand or fly, swelling in the head, neck and eyes, a twisted neck, and change in colour or cloudiness in the eyes, but warned some dead birds would be asymptomatic.

Deborah McSweyn is urging people to report cases of sick and dead birds. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

She said other animals could experience seizures, tremors, poor coordination, difficulty breathing, a runny nose and drooling.

As of Monday morning, there were 324 reports from across Tasmania.

To report sick or dead birds or other animals Call the ​ Emergency Animal Disease Hotline 1800 675 888 ​

Emergency Animal Disease Hotline Make an online report using one of the following reporting forms:​ Use the domestic and pet birds online form to report small numbers of sick or dead domestic or pet birds.​ Use the wild birds onlin​e form to report sick or dead wild birds, including native and non-native species. To report sick or dead wildlife (other than birds), please visit the wildlife health in Tasmania webpage. If you are reporting roadkill, please use the Tasmanian roadkill reporting form. If you are concerned about any other pet or animal you own, please contact your local veterinarian.

Tasmanian Aboriginal communities are also playing a part.

At Little Musselroe Bay, in Tasmania's far north-east, eight Tebrakunna rangers are stepping up beach patrols, ready to work with authorities if all turns "pear-shaped".

"I just thought, well, we might do a few more beach clean-ups, just to keep an eye on if birds are washing up, so we've been doing that," senior ranger Matt Cameron said.

"It will definitely be a big effort to keep on top of it."

Meanwhile, the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre has 45 Pakana rangers ready to assist across the state.

"We are concerned that the arrival of bird flu will impact one of our oldest cultural practices, the harvesting of yula/mutton birds," division manager culture and country Andry Sculthorpe said.

"It's hard to describe how significant this could be for our people. Muttonbirding is a cultural practice that has helped sustain us for millennia and survive the attempted genocide of our people."

Challenge for farmers

Tasmania's response team has also been working with poultry farmers to ensure they are ready to protect flocks against bird flu.

But it is particularly challenging for free-range producers, including Paul Hallier, who farms Muscovy ducks for meat at Birralee with his wife.

"We run an outside pasture-based system, so there is a limit to how feasible it is for us to get birds inside," he said.

"[Wild birds are] also just flying over the property; there is nothing to stop them pooing on the property as they go.

"We are feeding morning and night, which means that we're not leaving food out on pasture to encourage wild birds to come and visit, and only giving them enough food so that they eat it within sort of 10 to 15 minutes."

The farmer said he monitored birds daily, noting anything abnormal, and would inform authorities if there was a sudden influx of sick or dying birds.

"It would be shutting down the farm entirely, not letting anyone in and out and doing what they direct, which may just be isolating, it may be culling, we don't know until it turns up," he said.

World.title: Fires near Spokane, Washington destroy hundreds of buildings, force 60,000 evacuations
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaBushfires Fires near Spokane, Washington destroy hundreds of buildings, force 60,000 evacuations John Hanna Updated August 3, 2026 — 4:18pm ,first published August 2, 2026 — 4:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Topeka, Kansas: Wildfires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area while destroying at least 600 homes, businesses and other structures, authorities said on Sunday (Washington time). The fires in and around Spokane, the state’s second-largest city, burned about 21 square kilometres over the weekend and were among dozens of wildfires across the Western US that stretched the ability of federal, state and local agencies to fight them. Thousands of homes have been evacuated in Spokane with conditions forecast to deteriorate. AP Photo/Young Kwak A total of about 1000 square kilometres has burned across the state, and some of the fires, including those in the Spokane area, have not been contained. Fire and law enforcement officials said there had been no reports of injuries or people unaccounted for, but they stressed it was early in the response effort.



Officials also said the evacuees in Spokane included patients at its US Veterans Affairs hospital. Video from the Spokane area showed buildings on fire, black smoke billowing up near neighbourhoods, and the smoking ruins of homes, with only chimneys still standing. Several officials expressed concern that the area did not appear likely to get a break in coming days from the weather, which is expected to remain dry. The Old Trails fire burns near Spokane on Saturday. AP Photo/Young Kwak “We are not out of danger,” US senator Maria Cantwell said during a news conference with federal, state and local officials in Spokane. “The next couple of days will be challenging.” Investigators had yet to determine how the blazes started.



Spokane was hardly the only place struggling to contain fires. Related Article Exclusive

Bushfires ‘It looked like an atomic bomb’: The Aussie pilots flying into a French firestorm Crews using bulldozers and helicopters continued for a 10th day to fight a fire that has burned about 1360 square kilometres of grassland in western Idaho and eastern Oregon. The area is home to cattle ranches, and authorities said the fire was threatening more than 600 homes and 800 other structures. The weather in the area was expected to remain sunny and dry well into the week, with temperatures rising to more than 32 degrees Celsius on Wednesday. Officials say the fire was caused by lightning. In central Utah, a massive blaze more than doubled in size over the weekend, jumping from 41 square kilometres to about 145 square kilometres by Sunday morning. More than 100 cattle have been killed, according to local law enforcement.



Officials called the fire “catastrophic” as heavy winds helped flames jump containment lines overnight. The fire is moving north towards Fillmore, a town of about 2600 people and the seat of Millard County. Mandatory evacuations were ordered on Sunday evening for the southern portion of Fillmore. The National Weather Service issued warnings about the air quality across the north-west. It issued red-flag fire warnings for parts of Utah and Montana and western Nebraska, and extreme heat warnings for the southern parts of Arizona, California and Nevada and northern Montana. Fires fuelled by high temperatures and dry conditions have plagued the US Pacific Northwest for several months. Spokane Fire District 9 via AP While temperatures on Sunday in Spokane were forecast to remain below 27 C, wind gusts from 56km/h to 72km/h had been expected by the afternoon, said Benjamin Cossel, public information officer for the federal response team from California called on Saturday night to deal with the fires. “We have weather working against us, and we have terrain working against us,” Cossel said.



There were three fires in the Spokane area: the Old Trails Fire, the Fairview Fire and the Meadowview Fire. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson declared a state of emergency on Saturday, and the National Weather Service issued a “particularly dangerous situation” red flag alert for eastern Washington. Cossel said that as it got warmer during the day, cool air that was closer to the ground and keeping winds at bay would rise, allowing those winds to move through the area. The Spokane River cuts through the city of about 229,000 people, and there are steep canyons on both sides that channel the wind. Police block the road into an evacuation area in Spokane. AP Photo/Young Kwak “They push the fire through the canyons, up, up the slopes, and then outside the slopes and around,” he said. “It’s very, very hilly, very, very steep slopes, a lot of canyons that create really turbulent, really challenging sort of wind scenarios.” Authorities in Spokane set up a shelter at the city’s main convention centre. About 400 people were staying there, officials said on Sunday.



Spokane County commissioner Chris Jordan said relatives of his were in an area affected by the fires and that they did not know if their home was still standing. He said he spoke with them as they were leaving the home. Related Article Bushfires How extreme weather in Europe and North America is signalling a new era of fire danger for Australia “They’re in their car and all they can see is smoke everywhere, and it was incredibly scary for so many people,” he said during the news conference. Heather Rosenstrater, president and CEO of Avista Corp, the area’s electric and natural gas utility, said about 10,000 people were without power on Sunday, down from a peak of 30,000. Avista needed to repair two transmission lines, she said, so it was possible that demand for electricity over the next few days could cause outages. Meanwhile, several larger fires continued to burn in less populated areas north-west of Spokane, including one about 129 kilometres from the city that has burned about 544 square kilometres. Another fire in eastern Oregon, about 113 kilometres to the north-west in the Stinkingwater Mountains, has burned about 870 square kilometres.



“The whole north-west is heavily impacted right now,” said Keila Vizcarra, the spokesperson for the federal team from California handling what’s been named the Big Grass Fire in western Idaho and eastern Oregon. AP
