World.title: News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been gutted
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been gutted David Swan August 3, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Publishing giant News Corporation has attacked the federal government’s late changes to its plan to make tech giants pay for journalism, warning the revised design lets tech platforms off the hook just as the rules were meant to tighten. The blunt criticism from News Corp came as other publishers, including the owner of this masthead, Nine, were more measured in commenting on the changes, with Nine saying it was important the policy still met its purpose. The government is trying to ensure the sustainability of Australia’s media sector through the News Bargaining Incentive, a policy aimed at pushing tech giants to strike commercial deals with publishers. Minister for Communications and Minister for Sport Anika Wells and Assistant Treasurer and Minister for Financial Services Dr Daniel Mulino. Alex Ellinghausen The government on Monday confirmed tweaks to the policy, including narrowing the charge from the total Australian revenue of large tech platforms to their digital advertising revenue alone. To make up the difference, assistant treasurer Daniel Mulino said the rate would rise from 2.25 per cent to 2.5 per cent of the tech giant’s digital advertising revenue.



Platforms must also now strike deals with at least six publishers, up from the four proposed in April, and the carve-out for professional networking services such as Microsoft-owned LinkedIn is gone. Related Article News Bargaining Incentive Big carrot, more stick under news bargaining plan The incentive is the government’s answer to the failure of the 2021 news media bargaining code, which was meant to force Meta and Google to pay Australian publishers for the journalism circulating on their platforms. While Google signed deals, Meta walked away in 2024, and the code lacked the mechanisms to stop it. Publishers have long argued that tech giants pilfer the premium news content that is crucial to the success and user engagement of their networks. Tech companies, however, counter that publishers voluntarily share their articles to reap the commercial benefits of massive referral traffic, and argue that news actually makes up only a tiny fraction of what their users want to see. Nine Entertainment chief executive Matt Stanton said foreign-owned tech companies had a significant and growing influence over how Australians reached local journalism. Nine owns this masthead.



“These significant changes, made late in this process, require closer scrutiny to ensure it continues to meet its fundamental purpose: compelling these platforms to negotiate fairly for the journalism they benefit from,” he said. Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg. Bloomberg News Corp Australasia executive chairman Michael Miller went further, saying the changes “gut the incentive for tech platforms to strike fair deals with Australian media, right when those rules need strengthening, not softening”. “Tech giants cannot keep dodging their obligations. Australia deserves full revenue transparency, backed by severe, non-negotiable penalties for any platform that flouts local law,” he said. Mulino rejected the criticism, saying the money reaching media companies was unchanged. Fair commercial deals would deliver $200 million to $250 million a year, he said, while platforms that refused to negotiate would pay $350 million to $400 million.



“In the arrangements that we inherited there were few repercussions, if any, if big tech platforms walked away from news media organisations,” Mulino said. “Now, they will end up paying substantially more than if they enter into commercial agreements.” Rod Sims, the former Australian Competition and Consumer Commission chair who designed the original news media bargaining code, welcomed LinkedIn’s inclusion, but he did not follow the government’s arithmetic. The original code raised about $250 million five years ago, he said. The new scheme captures TikTok and LinkedIn on top of Meta and Google, yet the government is forecasting no more money than before. Sims also questioned how the charge treats Google’s search revenue as users migrate to Gemini summaries, saying it was not clear the interaction had been thought through. Mulino said the government had “consciously separated” AI from the incentive because a separate policy process looking at AI and copyright, led by the attorney-general. Scott Purcell, co-founder of Man of Many. Louise Kennerley



“What we’re looking at here is dealing with a situation where big tech platforms share news in its existing form,” he said. “There’s a separate process which is looking at the ways in which AI might manipulate or use the content of news to produce something new.” Independent publisher Man of Many, which in January was stripped from the government’s register of news businesses eligible under the scheme, said the changes improved the scheme but would reach almost none of the industry. Outlets that are not on the government’s register do not receive funding under the incentive. Co-founder Scott Purcell praised the grants program for the smallest publishers and the doubling of the loading for regional and diverse-community journalism. He said however that fewer than 100 businesses sit on ACMA’s register, while the same regulator’s media diversity framework counts 2864 professional news outlets. Australia accounts for about 2 per cent of global digital advertising, he said, and no platform will trade a global precedent for a discount in one mid-sized market. Meta, Google and TikTok declined to comment, while Microsoft and LinkedIn did not respond to requests for comment. Google has previously said it is the only tech company in Australia with commercial agreements supporting more than 90 news businesses. Meta abandoned its code-era deals in 2024 and has called the incentive a discriminatory tax, and it retains the option it has already used twice: stripping news from Facebook and Instagram, as it did in Canada in 2023 and briefly in Australia in 2021.



The bill is expected in parliament early in the spring sittings. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: David Hockney’s immersive display speaks to you ‘over your shoulder’
World.content:
CultureArt & designVisual art David Hockney’s immersive display speaks to you ‘over your shoulder’ Kayla Olaya August 3, 2026 — 3:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Months after his death, the voice of contemporary British artist David Hockney will guide audiences as they gaze upon walls emblazoned with colour, projecting his dreamy works at an upcoming art installation. One of his final projects, the immersive exhibition David Hockney: Bigger & Closer (not smaller & further away), will make its Australian debut at Sydney’s Carriageworks in October, following successful runs in London, Seoul, Singapore, Shanghai, Manchester and Aranya in China, during which about 650,000 people made their way through. Everleigh’s Carriageworks will stage David Hockney’s immersive light and audio experience. Sitthixay Ditthavong The installation plays recordings of Hockney’s voice dating back to his 20s and animates a selection of his works. But the painter wasn’t initially convinced by the idea, according to the man who helped bring the project to life. “We had to sort of persuade him to look back at past work,” said Richard Slaney, chief executive of Lightroom, which has partnered with Carriageworks to showcase the installation for its Australian debut.



“It’s not a full, complete biographical piece. But as a piece of legacy, I think what it does speak to is the philosophy behind this work about how to look at the world.” The display in London. Scale, light and perspective, elements from which Hockney, who died in June aged 88, drew inspiration across his long-spanning career, will be at the forefront of the installation. It is the second major Australian Hockney exhibition to open in the months after his death, with the National Gallery if Australia’s David Hockney: Portraits in Print opening on September 5. “It’s his work all around you, but also he’s narrating it, but in a way that your favourite relative would tell you something in an art gallery over your shoulder while you’re looking at that painting that brings it to life,” Slaney said.



Hockney taking a picture of a miniature version of the display. “It’s not scripted. It’s just, ‘Oh look at that. Look at this thing, and I did that’ … he was fascinated by the idea of reimagining his work in this way.” Opening on October 22 and running until January, the installation is broken into a series of chapters about different types of work in Hockney’s life, including one on opera paired with a score by Nic Muhly. Hockney inspected his installation. “There are chapters about music,” Carriageworks chief executive Fergus Linehan said. “There’s a chapter about lines, so they tend to be more based around ideas within his work, although it does go through different periods, like when he was young and went to Los Angeles.”



Related Article Art David Hockney was a painter of pools. I followed him into art’s deep end Coincidentally, the historic Sydney venue had a room with the exact dimensions needed to host the installation: 23 metres long, 15 metres wide and 10 metres high. Linehan’s vision for the installation aligns with one that he holds more broadly for Carriageworks, which he hopes can become “more of a public space”. “We’re here to make this building as useful as possible, and to make it busy and consistently in use … particularly during the day – it creates a kind of constant flow of people coming in,” he said. The 55-minute show is one anyone can enter at any time, Slaney said.

World.title: Wallabies, NRL or AFL? Tabuai-Fidow’s cross code dilemma as future call looms
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Wallabies, NRL or AFL? Tabuai-Fidow’s cross code dilemma as future call looms Nick Wright August 3, 2026 — 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow has confirmed his intent to remain in Dolphins colours and finish his career in the NRL, declaring he had no desire to return to the rival codes which made him one of the nation’s most elite athletes. While rugby league was ‘The Hammer’s’ first love, it was in Aussie rules and rugby union the Indigenous flyer appeared destined to make his mark. Initially a member of the Gold Coast Suns academy, Tabuai-Fidow eventually moved on a scholarship to Brisbane Grammar and linked up with the Queensland Reds’ academy. Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow and the Dolphins will wear their Indigenous Round jersey for the Battle of Brisbane. Fans get a glimpse of what he could have brought to the AFL whenever a midfield bomb goes up for the fullback to contest, but he says, “I think my AFL days are over, there’s a lot of running in that sport” when asked – in jest – if Karmichael Hunt-styled defection entertained his thoughts.



Blessed with pace shielded in mystique – the rhetoric being no one knew his top speed, as he was only ever as fast as he needed to be – a path to the Wallabies appeared to open up. In 2017, he scored 10 tries in a GPS First XV season, before he caught the eye of the North Queensland Cowboys. “I didn’t really know what to do at the time, I just went down for an opportunity on a scholarship and to play at a high level at that age. Then, when the Cowboys came knocking, that’s what I wanted to do,” Tabuai-Fidow said. “I was in the Reds academy, but there wasn’t too much happening at the time. I sort of didn’t really look into it that much, I just wanted to play my school footy. “[League] was the first sport that I did play at a young age, and watching all my uncles and my dad play, it was something I wanted to do. Having the chat with the Cowboys at the time, it was closer to home for myself as well, and I think that got me over.”



Tabuai-Fidow comes off contract with the Dolphins at the end of 2027, and will be free to negotiate with other outfits from November 1. But the 24-year-old insists his desire is to remain in Redcliffe, declaring he had not explored the prospect of following Angus Crichton, Joseph Aukuso-Suaalii and Mark Nawaqanitawase back to union. “My preference would be to stay here, but I’m not too worried about that. I’m just trying to get through each week, be with the boys and make this season a special one,” Tabuai-Fidow said. “I’m a league player for life now. It’s something that I still love and still enjoy doing, and I think that’s the most important thing … that’s what keeps me grounded.”



Fellow outside backs Herbie Farnworth, Selwyn Cobbo and Jack Bostock are in the same contract boat as Tabuai-Fidow, as the Dolphins wait to hear what the salary cap will be raised to after the NRL secured a landmark $5.3 billion broadcast deal to begin from 2028. While it is a lucrative list of retention priorities, they have money to spend given the losses of Kodi Nikorima (Dragons), Jake Averillo (Tigers), Oryn Keeley and Jamayne Isaako (Storm). Loading Daniel Saifiti was also forced into medical retirement due to ongoing issues with his shoulder, while England halfback George Williams stands as the Dolphins only 2027 recruit. And Tabuai-Fidow believes the rapport built between the squad and coach Kristian Woolf will serve as a retention weapon when the superstar quartet finalises their futures.



Related Article NRL 2026 No Dylans, no worries: Ponga pandemonium buries Broncos as a new star emerges During the Dolphins’ bye week before Friday’s 28-22 triumph of the Dragons, Woolf joined Tabuai-Fidow on a trip to Thursday Island to conduct school with the Torres Strait community. As he prepares to don the club’s Indigenous jersey for Saturday night’s Battle of Brisbane clash, the Maroons flyer revealed the way Woolf – who hails from Mount Isa – had developed a care for his players’ cultural backgrounds had been a key factor in his ability to get the best out of his squad. “Growing up with Indigenous boys and girls, he knows how to work us out and how to get the best out of us, and that’s something special to have,” Tabuai-Fidow said. “We can go into our shell and be pretty quiet, but I think we’re growing out of that as a culture – being proud, and Woolfy’s proud of that as well. It’s special to have that in a coach.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

The fire is moving north towards Fillmore, a town of about 2600 people and the seat of Millard County. Mandatory evacuations were ordered on Sunday evening for the southern portion of Fillmore. The National Weather Service issued warnings about the air quality across the north-west. It issued red-flag fire warnings for parts of Utah and Montana and western Nebraska, and extreme heat warnings for the southern parts of Arizona, California and Nevada and northern Montana. Fires fuelled by high temperatures and dry conditions have plagued the US Pacific Northwest for several months. Spokane Fire District 9 via AP While temperatures on Sunday in Spokane were forecast to remain below 27 C, wind gusts from 56km/h to 72km/h had been expected by the afternoon, said Benjamin Cossel, public information officer for the federal response team from California called on Saturday night to deal with the fires. “We have weather working against us, and we have terrain working against us,” Cossel said.



There were three fires in the Spokane area: the Old Trails Fire, the Fairview Fire and the Meadowview Fire. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson declared a state of emergency on Saturday, and the National Weather Service issued a “particularly dangerous situation” red flag alert for eastern Washington. Cossel said that as it got warmer during the day, cool air that was closer to the ground and keeping winds at bay would rise, allowing those winds to move through the area. The Spokane River cuts through the city of about 229,000 people, and there are steep canyons on both sides that channel the wind. Police block the road into an evacuation area in Spokane. AP Photo/Young Kwak “They push the fire through the canyons, up, up the slopes, and then outside the slopes and around,” he said. “It’s very, very hilly, very, very steep slopes, a lot of canyons that create really turbulent, really challenging sort of wind scenarios.” Authorities in Spokane set up a shelter at the city’s main convention centre. About 400 people were staying there, officials said on Sunday.



Spokane County commissioner Chris Jordan said relatives of his were in an area affected by the fires and that they did not know if their home was still standing. He said he spoke with them as they were leaving the home. Related Article Bushfires How extreme weather in Europe and North America is signalling a new era of fire danger for Australia “They’re in their car and all they can see is smoke everywhere, and it was incredibly scary for so many people,” he said during the news conference. Heather Rosenstrater, president and CEO of Avista Corp, the area’s electric and natural gas utility, said about 10,000 people were without power on Sunday, down from a peak of 30,000. Avista needed to repair two transmission lines, she said, so it was possible that demand for electricity over the next few days could cause outages. Meanwhile, several larger fires continued to burn in less populated areas north-west of Spokane, including one about 129 kilometres from the city that has burned about 544 square kilometres. Another fire in eastern Oregon, about 113 kilometres to the north-west in the Stinkingwater Mountains, has burned about 870 square kilometres.



“The whole north-west is heavily impacted right now,” said Keila Vizcarra, the spokesperson for the federal team from California handling what’s been named the Big Grass Fire in western Idaho and eastern Oregon. AP

World.title: News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been gutted
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been gutted David Swan August 3, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Publishing giant News Corporation has attacked the federal government’s late changes to its plan to make tech giants pay for journalism, warning the revised design lets tech platforms off the hook just as the rules were meant to tighten. The blunt criticism from News Corp came as other publishers, including the owner of this masthead, Nine, were more measured in commenting on the changes, with Nine saying it was important the policy still met its purpose. The government is trying to ensure the sustainability of Australia’s media sector through the News Bargaining Incentive, a policy aimed at pushing tech giants to strike commercial deals with publishers. Minister for Communications and Minister for Sport Anika Wells and Assistant Treasurer and Minister for Financial Services Dr Daniel Mulino. Alex Ellinghausen The government on Monday confirmed tweaks to the policy, including narrowing the charge from the total Australian revenue of large tech platforms to their digital advertising revenue alone. To make up the difference, assistant treasurer Daniel Mulino said the rate would rise from 2.25 per cent to 2.5 per cent of the tech giant’s digital advertising revenue.



Platforms must also now strike deals with at least six publishers, up from the four proposed in April, and the carve-out for professional networking services such as Microsoft-owned LinkedIn is gone. Related Article News Bargaining Incentive Big carrot, more stick under news bargaining plan The incentive is the government’s answer to the failure of the 2021 news media bargaining code, which was meant to force Meta and Google to pay Australian publishers for the journalism circulating on their platforms. While Google signed deals, Meta walked away in 2024, and the code lacked the mechanisms to stop it. Publishers have long argued that tech giants pilfer the premium news content that is crucial to the success and user engagement of their networks. Tech companies, however, counter that publishers voluntarily share their articles to reap the commercial benefits of massive referral traffic, and argue that news actually makes up only a tiny fraction of what their users want to see. Nine Entertainment chief executive Matt Stanton said foreign-owned tech companies had a significant and growing influence over how Australians reached local journalism. Nine owns this masthead.



“These significant changes, made late in this process, require closer scrutiny to ensure it continues to meet its fundamental purpose: compelling these platforms to negotiate fairly for the journalism they benefit from,” he said. Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg. Bloomberg News Corp Australasia executive chairman Michael Miller went further, saying the changes “gut the incentive for tech platforms to strike fair deals with Australian media, right when those rules need strengthening, not softening”. “Tech giants cannot keep dodging their obligations. Australia deserves full revenue transparency, backed by severe, non-negotiable penalties for any platform that flouts local law,” he said. Mulino rejected the criticism, saying the money reaching media companies was unchanged. Fair commercial deals would deliver $200 million to $250 million a year, he said, while platforms that refused to negotiate would pay $350 million to $400 million.



“In the arrangements that we inherited there were few repercussions, if any, if big tech platforms walked away from news media organisations,” Mulino said. “Now, they will end up paying substantially more than if they enter into commercial agreements.” Rod Sims, the former Australian Competition and Consumer Commission chair who designed the original news media bargaining code, welcomed LinkedIn’s inclusion, but he did not follow the government’s arithmetic. The original code raised about $250 million five years ago, he said. The new scheme captures TikTok and LinkedIn on top of Meta and Google, yet the government is forecasting no more money than before. Sims also questioned how the charge treats Google’s search revenue as users migrate to Gemini summaries, saying it was not clear the interaction had been thought through. Mulino said the government had “consciously separated” AI from the incentive because a separate policy process looking at AI and copyright, led by the attorney-general. Scott Purcell, co-founder of Man of Many. Louise Kennerley



“What we’re looking at here is dealing with a situation where big tech platforms share news in its existing form,” he said. “There’s a separate process which is looking at the ways in which AI might manipulate or use the content of news to produce something new.” Independent publisher Man of Many, which in January was stripped from the government’s register of news businesses eligible under the scheme, said the changes improved the scheme but would reach almost none of the industry. Outlets that are not on the government’s register do not receive funding under the incentive. Co-founder Scott Purcell praised the grants program for the smallest publishers and the doubling of the loading for regional and diverse-community journalism. He said however that fewer than 100 businesses sit on ACMA’s register, while the same regulator’s media diversity framework counts 2864 professional news outlets. Australia accounts for about 2 per cent of global digital advertising, he said, and no platform will trade a global precedent for a discount in one mid-sized market. Meta, Google and TikTok declined to comment, while Microsoft and LinkedIn did not respond to requests for comment. Google has previously said it is the only tech company in Australia with commercial agreements supporting more than 90 news businesses. Meta abandoned its code-era deals in 2024 and has called the incentive a discriminatory tax, and it retains the option it has already used twice: stripping news from Facebook and Instagram, as it did in Canada in 2023 and briefly in Australia in 2021.



The bill is expected in parliament early in the spring sittings. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: David Hockney’s immersive display speaks to you ‘over your shoulder’
World.content:
CultureArt & designVisual art David Hockney’s immersive display speaks to you ‘over your shoulder’ Kayla Olaya August 3, 2026 — 3:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Months after his death, the voice of contemporary British artist David Hockney will guide audiences as they gaze upon walls emblazoned with colour, projecting his dreamy works at an upcoming art installation. One of his final projects, the immersive exhibition David Hockney: Bigger & Closer (not smaller & further away), will make its Australian debut at Sydney’s Carriageworks in October, following successful runs in London, Seoul, Singapore, Shanghai, Manchester and Aranya in China, during which about 650,000 people made their way through. Everleigh’s Carriageworks will stage David Hockney’s immersive light and audio experience. Sitthixay Ditthavong The installation plays recordings of Hockney’s voice dating back to his 20s and animates a selection of his works. But the painter wasn’t initially convinced by the idea, according to the man who helped bring the project to life. “We had to sort of persuade him to look back at past work,” said Richard Slaney, chief executive of Lightroom, which has partnered with Carriageworks to showcase the installation for its Australian debut.



“It’s not a full, complete biographical piece. But as a piece of legacy, I think what it does speak to is the philosophy behind this work about how to look at the world.” The display in London. Scale, light and perspective, elements from which Hockney, who died in June aged 88, drew inspiration across his long-spanning career, will be at the forefront of the installation. It is the second major Australian Hockney exhibition to open in the months after his death, with the National Gallery if Australia’s David Hockney: Portraits in Print opening on September 5. “It’s his work all around you, but also he’s narrating it, but in a way that your favourite relative would tell you something in an art gallery over your shoulder while you’re looking at that painting that brings it to life,” Slaney said.



Hockney taking a picture of a miniature version of the display. “It’s not scripted. It’s just, ‘Oh look at that. Look at this thing, and I did that’ … he was fascinated by the idea of reimagining his work in this way.” Opening on October 22 and running until January, the installation is broken into a series of chapters about different types of work in Hockney’s life, including one on opera paired with a score by Nic Muhly. Hockney inspected his installation. “There are chapters about music,” Carriageworks chief executive Fergus Linehan said. “There’s a chapter about lines, so they tend to be more based around ideas within his work, although it does go through different periods, like when he was young and went to Los Angeles.”



Related Article Art David Hockney was a painter of pools. I followed him into art’s deep end Coincidentally, the historic Sydney venue had a room with the exact dimensions needed to host the installation: 23 metres long, 15 metres wide and 10 metres high. Linehan’s vision for the installation aligns with one that he holds more broadly for Carriageworks, which he hopes can become “more of a public space”. “We’re here to make this building as useful as possible, and to make it busy and consistently in use … particularly during the day – it creates a kind of constant flow of people coming in,” he said. The 55-minute show is one anyone can enter at any time, Slaney said.

World.title: Almost a million cervical cancer screening notifications not sent out, review finds
World.content:
Almost a million notifications did not get sent to people eligible for cancer screening due to flaws in the national cervical cancer screening programme, a review has found.

As a result, the system was not providing a comprehensive safety net.

A national register was launched in September 2023, along with a change to HPV primary screening instead of a smear test.

A review by a Health New Zealand expert panel, released on Monday, said the register was working satisfactorily in many ways but the clinical safety of the register could not be assured in some situations.

The register was not making contact with everyone eligible for screening due to the way it was designed, as well as unintentional flaws in the way it was built, the review said.

More than 800,000 notifications for screening were not triggered and another 160,000 notifications were triggered but not sent as of June 2025.

That included more than 600,000 notifications not sent or triggered due to people considered "inactive" because of Health NZ's "NHI active rule" that meant people who had not accessed health services for three years were not sent cervical screening eligibility information.

Others were not contacted due to postal addressees being incorrect or lacking.

A process aimed at prioritising those most in need - referred to as cohorting - also resulted in people only in the most high-priority group being contacted.

Eligibility and recall notifications were only sent to people in Cohort One - people ageing into the scheme and unscreened or underscreened Māori or Pacific people who were not enrolled in primary care.

The review made 48 recommendations, including identifying and contacting all unscreened and under-screened people as a priority.

The system needed to ensure there was appropriate follow-up when screening detected abnormalities, it said.

The register does not currently have access to complete screening histories for all participants.

This meant it might not be able to determine next steps and if additional work was required to review participants with complex histories, including previous high-grade results or other persistent HPV infections to ensure they were receiving appropriate care, the review said.

"Failure to do so poses a significant risk to affected individuals, potentially leading to delayed diagnosis or treatment and so proactive measures must be taken to safeguard patient outcomes," it said.

The review called for the National Cervical Screening Programme and Health NZ's Digital Services to develop an action plan to address the issues identified by the notification review.

National Public Health Service director prevention screening Alana Ewe-Snow said it was grateful to the work of the panel in identifying the areas for improvement.

"We acknowledge there is further work to do to improve the register. We are working hard to address the panel's recommendations. The main recommendations centred around improving clinical case review, data quality and notifications to women," Dr Ewe-Snow said.

Screening rates were higher than ever with increases across all ethnicities following the introduction of HPV primary screening with more than a million people screened since the register was introduced in September 2023, she said.

"This progress is heartening but there is much more work to do. Improvements to the register will mean we can reach even more women for screening. We'll be able to support more women to progress through the screening assessment and treatment pathway earlier."

There had been 13,000 case reviews and so far there was no indication anyone had been harmed as a result of the system's issues, Dr Ewe-Snow said.

World.title: CCTV shown at inquest into Isaac Levings' death after he fell in Wellington Harbour
World.content:
A Wellington court has been shown CCTV footage leading up to the moment Christchurch teacher Isaac Levings fell into Wellington Harbour and drowned in 2023.

Levings disappeared from Queens Wharf after attending a concert by pop rock band, The 1975 at TSB Arena in April 2023.

His body was found in the water near Te Papa two days later.

Presiding over the inquest into Levings' death on Monday, Coroner Katharine Greig said there had been more than half a dozen deaths involving people falling into the harbour since 2015 - including that of Wellington man Sandy Calkin.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Calkin's death - which was the subject of a previous inquest in 2024 - resulted in six recommendations to the council to improve safety along the waterfront.

Counsel for the coroner, Josh Shaw told the court the inquest into Levings' death was an opportunity to examine council progress on improving safety on the Wellington waterfront.

Shaw told the court the work to improve lighting along the promenade had been well advanced and proposals to improve edge protection had progressed towards public consultation.

"There was a will to continue this... and make sure that all that could be done was done to enhance safety at the waterfront," Shaw said.

Counsel for the coroner, Josh Shaw RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But he said a council proposal to proceed with edge protection measures near where Calkin had died and on the wider waterfront was voted down by council in August 2025.

"And so we are left, currently at least, with a waterfront with much better lighting - including at the Te Papa promenade where the lighting was not good at the time of Isaac's death - but has since been significantly upgraded.

"But a waterfront that has virtually no edge protection - at least across the majority of it. Including - because a couple of months after that August decision - there was also a decision to remove temporary fencing that had been installed pending a more long term solution," Shaw said.

Shaw said the inquest would examine the circumstances of Levings' death and also the processes by which the previous recommendations had "landed where they have".

A clever, quick witted teacher 'adored' by his students

Family of the deceased at the coronial inquest following the death of 25-year-old Issac Levings RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Today's inquest was attended by Isaac Levings' parents, Charles and Margaret Levings and his older brother James Levings.

Charles Levings described his son as a clever, quick witted and intelligent young man who was "adored" by his young students.

"At morning tea time, he was out on the field playing with the children - very rarely went into the staff room for morning tea - he would be out there on the fields. He understood children so much," Charles Levings said.

Charles Levings went to pains to express to the court that the level of intoxication illustrated by CCTV footage of the night of Levings death was out of character.

"For him to be intoxicated, as he was, was a surprise to me personally as his dad. I'd never seen him drink to that kind of level."

Isaac Levings' father Charles Levings at the inquest. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

CCTV tracks Levings along waterfront promenade

The Court was shown CCTV footage of Levings as he made his way south along the waterfront promenade after leaving the TSB Arena.

Levings could be seen in a stained grey T-shirt and shorts following a meandering path along the waterfront.

He posture was loose and he occasionally steadied himself against the wall and construction barriers along the waterfront edge of Frank Kitts Park.

Footage showed Levings crossing the bridge near the Taranaki Street diving platform as he walked along the Ara Moana walkway opposite Te Papa .

Soon after a splash and eddies could be seen on the calm surface of the harbour - emanating outwards from the wharfs edge at around 10.46 pm.

Daniel Bayliss went to the concert with Levings and some other friends that night.

He told the court the group had each bought ten packs of RTDs - consuming them before they arrived at the venue - and Levings purchased several more red wines as the concert progressed.

The Wellington waterfront moments after 25-year-old Issac Levings fell in 2023 RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said the last he saw of Levings was when he popped briefly into toilets as Bayliss was using them.

Bayliss said repeated messages and calls to Levings phone following that point went unanswered and unread.

Security staff member says she had 'a gut feeling' seeing Levings outside venue.

Louise Torres was working with the Red Badge security team at the venue that night.

She outlined the responsibilities and powers of the security teams stationed at the venue including being on the lookout for intoxicated concert goers and potentially evicting them from the venue as well as arranging transport or assistance for people deemed "at risk".

She said some time after 8.30 pm she was alerted to a concert goer with vomit on his shirt who turned out to be Levings.

"He had slurred speech, was unable to stand up straight and had bloodshot eyes," Torres said.

She said security staff supervised a chill out room where people might be taken, or go voluntarily, if they needed to sober up or "if they are feeling overwhelmed, too drunk or need to take a break".

Torres said she understood Levings' degree of intoxication would be assessed by paramedics or security staff in the chill out area.

Torres would later see Levings holding himself up on a pillar outside the venue but he "waived off" her attempt to speak with him.

"I remember thinking that Isaac still seemed drunk and having a gut feeling about him."

Torres told the court she later contacted police when she realised the same man she had interactions with was missing and told them she was concerned he had fallen in the water.

Wellington Free Ambulance Head of Event Medical Services and paramedic, Daniel Ashcroft told the court he was among six ambulance staff working at the concert.

Ashcroft said it had taken a wheelchair to assist Levings from the crowd but - in a better ventilated assessment room - and he was able to walk, talk and hold a conversation.

He said Levings had declined a more thorough assessment saying he had "only been drinking".

Ashcroft said he was called away to assist other patrons and on his return he was told Levings had been escorted out of the building by security staff.

"The reasons for his removal by security are unknown to me," Ashcroft said.

World.title: Schools close roads to make drop-offs safer: 'It felt very chaotic'
World.content:
Primary schools say a pilot programme that allows them to close nearby roads during drop off and pick up times is helping to curb dangerous driver's behaviour.

It has been a growing issue in New Zealand's biggest city, with Auckland Transport starting Safe School Streets a couple of years ago.

The programme has been testing how to manage safety, cut peak traffic and encourage walking or cycling at 13 schools.

But other schools across Aotearoa are facing the same issues and some are taking matters into their own hands.

At 8.30am outside Freeman's Bay school in central Auckland, cars were queuing up and were getting as close as they could to the school's gates.

Children were beginning to walk across the zebra crossing, with commuters speeding past on their way to work.

Checkpoint spoke with some parents who had found a park about the behaviour they had seen over the past few months.

"We have had a car accident because just up here someone had done a U-turn in front of us and didn't see us," said one parent.

"I've seen people kind of flip around, do a U-turn to get from one side to the other and on the other side are little kids who run around," said another.

Schools struggle with dangerous driving during drop off and pick up Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

A school in Christchurch has been facing the same problem as its entrance is in the middle of a busy cul-de-sac.

Waimairi School principal Chris Panther said parents had been parking on yellow lines on both sides of the road and over driveways on Tillman Avenue.

"It felt very chaotic, we had students biking to school, scootering and walking.

"As I watched outside my office, there was always the worry someone was going to back out of their driveway, [with] children crossing across the cul-de-sac."

To counter the problem, with permission from the council, Waimairi School has started closing the road during peak pick up and drop off times.

A teacher kept an eye on the barrier, to make sure residents on the street and emergency services could still get through.

Panther said it had been a game changer.

"Now, it feels very calm, very orderly, we've got a care crossing operating on Blighs Road that also feels much calmer now because we're only dealing with traffic in one direction.

"We've opened up another gate at the back of our school

In partnership with the Christchurch City Council, the school will trial the closures until the end of the year.

It will then reassess whether the change will become permanent.

"We were concerned about moving the problem to other surrounding streets, so the council's been out with us as has the local police and parking wardens.

"Over the last week or so they've been checking those streets so Blighs Road, Windermere Road, Condell Avenue and Westholme Street, they're all looking reasonable."

File photo. RNZ / Amy Williams

Waimairi School got the idea from Marlborough Primary School in Auckland's Glenfield.

It was the first school to introduce restrictions under Waka Kotahi's Reshaping Streets regulations in March last year.

Principal Michelle Nell said drivers were having regular near misses with students.

"It was chaos, it was parents behaving very badly and not thinking about their own child's safety.

"They would come into the road and stop wherever they wanted to, open the doors let the kids out in the middle of the road and get really upset because people were blocking them getting out.

"Neighbours were [also] upset about cars blocking the driveways, so they couldn't get out to work."

Nell said because parents now must park further away from the school, it had cleared the roads for students trying to walk.

After surveying the community, Auckland Transport found 82 percent of parents and 90 percent of teachers thought safety had improved.

"Getting our kids safely to school is paramount. I would say just do it, do what you feel is best.

"If somebody comes and complains, tell them that you're doing it for the kids and 99 percent of the time they'll turn around and say, good on you."

But not everyone is sold.

Amy Manos, the deputy principal of Rosebank School in West Auckland, said closing the road would be ideal.

But she said it was not realistic for some schools who were on busy main routes, who shared the road with commuters and industrial traffic.

"A kiss and drop zone would be perfect.

"That's what parents ultimately want to do, is to drive into a safe space, give their kids a kiss, wave goodbye and know that they're safe on the school grounds."

World.title: All Interislander sailings cancelled tomorrow due to expected bad weather
World.content:
All Interislander sailings have been cancelled tomorrow, due to forecast high winds and large swells.

Four Interislander sailings between Wellington and Picton were cancelled due to a forecast southerly weather system in the Cook Strait.

Interislander said the safety of passengers and crew was its top priority.

"All affected passengers are being moved to alternative sailings and are being contacted directly."

Bluebridge has cancelled all services but its 2am Wellington to Picton sailing and 2.30am Picton to Wellington sailing on Tuesday.

"All affected customers have been contacted by email and/or text and moved to the next available sailing once it is safe to resume passenger services."

World.title: The Silver Ferns won Commonwealth Games gold, but a bigger fight is just beginning
World.content:
Grace Nweke turns her Commonwealth Games gold medal over in her hands, studying it intently, before letting it fall back against her chest.

Half an hour earlier, the star shooter had been in tears in the centre of Glasgow's The Hydro arena as she embraced her team-mates in the emotional celebrations that followed Silver Ferns' stunning win over Jamaica in the Commonwealth Games netball final.

The win - which ended a 16-year drought for New Zealand in the pinnacle event - came off the back of one of the most turbulent years any Silver Ferns team has had to endure.

Now, talking to reporters with a gold medal around her neck and the noise of the final beginning to fade, Nweke is only just starting to process the journey that had brought the Silver Ferns to this moment.

"It's really heavy," she says of her new golden accessory. "I've never had one before."

Over the past 12 months Nweke and her national teammates have carried a different kind of weight.

They have lost their captain, Ameliaranne Ekenasio, who elected to step away from the team last year, saying she needed a break "for my mind, body and spirit".

They have seen coach Dame Noeline Taurua stood down by the national body after what began as a discreet cultural review of the Ferns' environment erupted into a bitter employment dispute.

Then, in the fallout that followed Taurua's shock suspension, they have listened as former players bagged them and questioned their professionalism.

Star shooter Grace Nweke was a rock under the goal for New Zealand all tournament. Jayne Russell / www.photosport.nz

And they have been picked apart on talkback radio, on social media and in comment sections, becoming the target of relentless criticism.

Hanging over all of it has been questions about the future of the domestic game.

With no broadcast deal in place for next season, Netball NZ is yet to commit to running a competition in 2027, which left many in the team heading into the tournament not knowing whether they will have a professional contract next season.

Somehow, everything that threatened to consume them off the court never followed them onto it.

"There were definitely moments where you questioned what you're doing and I think it took more of a toll than I've processed," says Nweke.

"I think I got to a point where I was like it's got to count for something. I'm really grateful to seal off this story with this gold."

The eight-goal win over Jamaica on Monday morning capped off a near-flawless campaign for the Silver Ferns, built on precision rather than emotion.

Throughout the week the Ferns had made no secret of the ambitious target they set for themselves of limiting turnovers to fewer than 10 per game. On Monday, against a Jamaican side known for its defensive clout, the New Zealand side's error count was just eight for the entire game - virtually unheard of in international netball, let alone in the cauldron of a championship final at the end of a run of seven games in 10 days.

Much of that composure bore the hallmarks of Taurua.

Quietly going about her business with minimal fuss throughout the tournament, the veteran coach - who famously led the Ferns to a World Cup title in 2019 after 11 months in charge - once again showed her ability to mold a team in a short space of time.

"The game plan speaks for itself, she's a mastermind and we're very lucky to have her," Nweke said of her coach.

For many, the gold medal will inevitably be viewed as a measure of vindication for Taurua after a tumultuous 2025, but the coach herself was reluctant to entertain such questions - only going as far to say that the victory was "sweet".

"What doesn't kill you makes you stronger, so it's very cool," said Taurua.

"It's an honour for me to be able to be back with the Silver Ferns and coach them, it's sweet getting gold and I'm absolutely proud of the players, the staff, and our whole team."

For the Silver Ferns team and coaching staff, the gold medal offers a powerful sense of closure after a turbulent year. But it does not provide a fairytale ending for the sport.

There remain genuine fears for the future of New Zealand's elite domestic competition, after Netball NZ revealed it is forecasting a loss of up to $6 million for the financial year - $3.7m can be attributed to the costs of running the ANZ Premiership.

An emotional Grace Nweke hugs teammate Kelly Jackson following the Ferns' stunning win. Jayne Russell / Photosport

As it battles to secure broadcast and commercial investment, it is understood Netball NZ is considering putting the ANZ Premiership competition on hold, or returning to an amateur one. The uncertainty has forced the national body to scrap the final restrictions preventing Silver Ferns and other leading players from pursuing overseas contracts.

Silver Ferns captain Karin Burger, who is one of nine New Zealand players already to make the leap and take up contracts in Australia's Suncorp Super Netball this season, says she has been sad to see what has happened to the New Zealand league over the past few years.

She hopes the team's performance in Glasgow in the face of huge adversity would become part of the argument for investing in the game.

"I think it shows the strength of the women in our sport and what we are capable of doing. Hopefully that shines the light on us, and the product that we do have and that we continuously can put out there regardless of what's thrown our way."

For Mila Reuelu-Buchanan, the breakout star of the Ferns' campaign, the moment carried an even wider significance.

Before the tournament, the midcourter was among a group of senior players leading calls for greater support for netball in New Zealand. After Monday's match, an emotional Reuelu-Buchanan once again gave an impassioned plea.

"This medal is also for netball in New Zealand. Currently there is no competition, and that's the reality. It's really hard to believe that the future is uncertain for us. I hope there is someone back home who sees the real potential in our sport because it needs to stay alive," she said.

"This is for those that have gone before us and it also shows there is a future here waiting for us.

"We've had to play in this competition with real uncertainty about our livelihoods, and that gave us extra strength and mana to play for each other."

Somewhere in amongst the dysfunction, the Silver Ferns found the togetherness to survive.

World.title: Luxon speaks to Peters about comments: 'That's a conversation between us'
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he has had a conversation with Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters, following his tirade towards a Chinese-born MP in Parliament last week.

New Zealand First's leader responded to heckling in the House on Wednesday last week by attacking the Greens' Lawrence Xu-nan, telling him to go back to his own country.

Earlier Monday morning, Luxon confirmed to Morning Report he had not yet spoken to Peters directly, but said the comments were racist.

Speaking at the post-cab media conference on Monday afternoon, Luxon said he had spoken to Peters, but refused to outline what exactly was discussed, nor would he say whether he expressed disappointment in his foreign minister.

"My conversation will stay between Winston and me," said Luxon.

"I've addressed it. I've had a conversation with Winston. That's a conversation between us."

Asked why he did not contact Peters over the weekend, Luxon said it was better "when we're in person in a place like this on a Monday".

"It worked better for us to have a quick chat."

Asked directly whether Peters was acting professionally according to the Cabinet Manual, Luxon repeated again that he'd had a conversation with Peters and it would stay between them.

Luxon reiterated his view the comments were offensive and unacceptable, and suggested if people feel that language was unacceptable to "party vote National".

He also said it was his view Peters should apologise, "but it's up to him to determine what he wants to do".

Luxon would not say if he would have Peters as foreign minister again if he won the election, saying that was all "hypothetical", nor would he be drawn on questions about the risk to coalition stability if Luxon were to discipline or try fire Peters.

Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty said Luxon should sack Peters because he had "embarrassed the country" and offended the largest trading partner.

"I reckon he'd look like he's actually grown a pair by dealing with someone that has seriously jeopardised an important relationship with our largest trading partner."

He said it "doesn't wash" that the prime minister said he'd had a conversation with Peters and it would stay between them.

"What I think actually happened is Luxon asked for a conversation, Winston laughed in his face and walked away.

"That's why they're keeping it quiet because it didn't go very well for Christopher Luxon."

He stopped short of ruling Peters out as a future foreign minister under a Labour-led government, saying it was not his job as a spokesperson, but reiterated that leader Chris Hipkins had said he would sack Peters for making those comments if he was foreign minister in his government.

World.title: 'A possible early warning signal' - volcanic activity increases beneath Mt Ruapehu
World.content:
Scientists are monitoring Mount Ruapehu after an increase in volcanic activity has been detected.

It is in a state of minor unrest, with the constant tremor beneath the volcano having increased from a weak to moderate level.

Geologist Michael Rosenberg said it could be an early warning sign of an eruption.

There had been a gradual increase in the volcanic tremor since 22 July, Rosenberg said, which had reached a level that had not been recorded in at least two years.

"It doesn't, by itself, mean that the volcano is going to erupt.

"It's more like a possible early warning signal."

Rosenberg said there had been a minimal change in temperature at Crater Lake, or Te Wai ā-moe, which remained stable.

The output of gas emissions, such as volcanic sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide, were still at a low-to-moderate amount.

Rosenberg said the tremor was also within the range expected during minor unrest.

He said there was no link between New Zealand's heightened seismic activity, and an increase in the level of volcanic tremor beneath Mount Ruapehu.

World.title: Popular Auckland marine reserve Goat Island the next site for paid parking
World.content:
Paid parking will be introduced Auckland's popular marine reserve Goat Island in Leigh, the Department of Conservation (DOC) says.

It followed paid parking being introduced at three popular South Island tourist destinations - Punakaiki, Franz Josef and Aoraki Mt Cook.

DOC said paid parking was a tool used globally to support conservation by managing visitor numbers and generating revenue to contribute to the financial sustainability of popular natural and historic sites.

Its Auckland Operations Director Alex Roger, said Goat Island was one of DOC's most popular sites.

"International visitors and kiwis flock to the site in summer, connecting with a flourishing underwater world. We love seeing the place full, but it does put huge pressure on the three car park areas, toilet and changing block, and wider area."

Paid parking was aimed to be introduced in December, Rogers said and would help manage congestion, encourage turnover of the limited car parks available, and raise revenue for conservation.

The revenue would be reinvested into regional and national conservation areas, he said.

"In August we're engaging with the local community to get feedback on the pricing structure, and working on defining the boundary of local catchment area as those within it will be able to apply for annual permits, we want to make sure we get those things right."

World.title: NRLW star in hot water for dangerous lifting tackle
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos NRLW star Ali Brigginshaw is facing the prospect of a lengthy stint on the sidelines after being referred straight to the judiciary for a lifting tackle during last weekend's Magic Round.

The Broncos remained unbeaten and on top of the ladder with a commanding 34-4 victory over the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs, but the win was soured by Brigginshaw's first-half tackle on Bulldogs halfback Tayla Preston.

Brigginshaw was sent to the sin bin after her tackle on Preston, where the Bulldogs player was swung around and lifted before being driven into the ground head-first.

Preston avoided serious injury, and Brigginshaw was handed a grade three dangerous throw charge.

The 36-year-old, who is playing her final season of NRLW before retirement, has never missed a Broncos game since the competition's inception in 2018.

She will argue her case at the judiciary on Tuesday, where she could face a significant ban.

Sydney Roosters forward Aliyah Nasio was the last NRLW player to be referred directly to the judiciary following a brawl at the conclusion of last year's grand final, where she struck Brisbane's Julia Robinson.

Nasio was banned for four matches after being hit with a grade three striking charge.

Brisbane, reigning NRLW premiers, faces Canberra this week, followed by a grand final rematch with the Roosters, then a derby against the Gold Coast Titans.

World.title: Canberra secures new NBL role amid expansion team hopes
World.content:
Canberra is one step closer to hosting an NBL team for the first time in more than two decades, the league's parent company chief executive has said.

The NBL's in-season competition, the Ignite Cup, will undergo a shake-up with the tournament's finals set to move from the Gold Coast to Canberra's AIS Arena.

It is the latest competition development in the nation's capital as speculation grows that the league is looking to expand into Canberra along with Darwin, the Gold Coast and a second Sydney team.

Ingles comes 'home' in coup NBL signing The legendary Boomers and NBA star will return to Australia's NBL for the first time since 2009, signing with Melbourne United for two years.

Competition executives have said they want to grow the current 10-team league, but new clubs will have to have the capacity to host at least 8,000 spectators.

With the ACT government announcing it will build the Canberra Convention and Entertainment precinct, hope remains the city can secure an NBL team for the first time since the Canberra Cannons were last involved in 2003.

The Cannons won three NBL titles before relocating to Newcastle, while the Sydney Kings now play some regular season matches at AIS Arena.

Admitting he would have loved to announce a Cannons rebirth on Monday, NBL Group CEO David Stevenson still gave every indication the league was eyeing the capital.

"We've got strong confidence that we can work together with Basketball ACT, with everyone involved in the sport to make sure that hopefully once the venue gets approved, that we can build a great team," he said.

"What we're building is a really strong business case, and it's not just about what happens at the game; it's the economic contribution that's really important for us."

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr added that a minimum of 7,500 seats were planned for the Canberra Convention and Entertainment precinct.

"A key element of the business case is having a basketball team play there, or more than one basketball team, actually. But it's not just a basketball stadium, it's got to accommodate other uses as well," Barr said.

"The AIS Arena is a fantastic venue, but it sort of maxes out at about 5,000 people.

"It was very clear in talking both to live music promoters, to the major sporting organisations … that we were missing out because 5,000 was too small."

But before expansion, the nation's capital will have to settle for the midweek Ignite Cup, an NBL competition involving 20 games held on Wednesday nights.

The four most successful teams will compete for a share in $550,000 when they progress to the semifinals in Canberra on February 19 before the decider on February 21.

The NBL's MVP Awards are also moving from Melbourne for the first time in more than a decade and will be hosted at the Great Hall in Canberra's Parliament House.

AAP

World.title: McIlroy headlines summer of golf with DeChambeau targeted
World.content:
The return of grand slam winner Rory McIlroy and the first Australian PGA Championship in Sydney this century highlights a 19-event summer of golf starting this month.

With the global professional golf scene in a state of flux, the Australasian Tour has secured a record partnership and announced a jam-packed schedule with major championship and European Tour spots once again up for grabs.

McIlroy back gracing Melbourne fairways, this time at iconic Kingston Heath from December 3–6, and the PGA Championship at The Lakes possibly featuring big-hitting fan favourite Bryson DeChambeau, are the two hottest tickets.

McIlroy completes one of his missions Rory McIlroy's appearance at the Australian Open in Melbourne has gone a long way to restoring the prestige of the tournament.

Record crowds followed the Northern Irishman at last year's Australian Open at Royal Melbourne before McIlroy successfully defended his US Masters title at Augusta National in April.

Officials revealed they were also targeting two-time US Open winner DeChambeau for the PGA, which was last held in Sydney back in 1998.

The new season begins in the now traditional style with the PNG Open at Royal Port Moresby Golf Club on August 27–30 before visiting all mainland states in Australia, as well as New Zealand's north and south islands, across the 19-tournament schedule.

The centenary Queensland PGA Championship will take place on the Kurrai course at Nudgee Golf Club in Brisbane from November 19–22.

Boasting a past champions list that includes Australian greats Greg Norman, David Graham and Peter Senior, the event will be played immediately before the Australian PGA Championship.

Co-sanctioned by the European Tour, the Australian PGA Championship also marks the start of the Race to Dubai, the tour's season-long rankings competition.

The PGA Tour of Australasia will also feature two new tournament venues in 2026–27.

Secret Harbour Golf Links, south of Perth, will host the WA Open for the first time, while Peninsula Kingswood Country Golf Club becomes the new home of Players Series Victoria as a forerunner to hosting next year's Australian Open.

There is a switch of order for the three-leg New Zealand swing in February that proved to be a huge success in 2026.

The New Zealand Open will now be the finale, following the Japan-Australasia Championship that returns for its second year at Royal Auckland & Grange Golf Club.
